paragraphs.text: 7.2-13 A lawyer who comes into possession of a privileged communication of an opposing party must not make use of it and must immediately advise the opposing lawyer or opposing party. The Commentary to the Code of Conduct continues: [2] Immediately upon realizing that the communication is a privileged communication of another party, the lawyer shall not continue to read the communication and must bring it to the attention of opposing counsel, then return or destroy it, without copies having been made. Knowledge that a communication is not intended for the lawyer receiving it will be imputed if, under the circumstances, it would have been unreasonable for the lawyer to come to any other conclusion. … [4] In the event there is a genuine dispute over the nature of the communication, it shall be permissible for the receiving lawyer to secure the communication, pending resolution of the dispute. The issue of whether or to what extent the communication may be copied or its contents disclosed or used must be resolved by agreement or by the court. In the meantime, it is improper to use the communication or disclose its contents in any manner. 16. Similar Fact Evidence In N. (K.) v. Alberta (1999), 243 A.R. 94 (Q.B.), the plaintiff in a wrongful sexual sterilization action against the Province of Alberta sought production of certain records on the basis that they contained similar fact evidence. Wachowich A.C.J.Q.B. held that the concept of similar fact evidence applied to civil proceedings, but that the test differed from that used in the criminal law. As there is little law in Alberta on this topic, his Lordship's detailed analysis is worth repeating. At pp. 98-107, his Lordship said: The admissibility of similar fact evidence is an exception to the general exclusionary rule of evidence which prohibits a party from adducing evidence of the bad character of the opposite party to prove or disprove a fact in issue. Put simply, the exclusionary rule is that it is insufficient and dangerous to determine civil or criminal liability on no more than a person's general disposition, habit or propensity to be a bad actor… Stated another way, which is perhaps the best way of approaching similar fact evidence in the context of discovery where relevance is the primary criterion, Phipson on Evidence (14th Ed.) (London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1990) begins with the principle that everything relevant should be admitted, and then subjects that rule to two exceptions, excluding relevant information where this would prove no more than a propensity to be a bad actor or to act like other bad actors in similar circumstances (at p. 373): Subject to two exceptions stated below, evidence of facts or transactions similar to the fact or transaction directly in issue is admissible if it is logically probative, that is if it is logically relevant in determining the matter which is in issue (Per Lord Denning, M.R., in Mood Music Publishing Co. Ltd. v. de Wolfe Ltd., [1976] 2 W.L.R. 451, 456 (C.A.)), and it is not otherwise excluded, e.g., by the rule against hearsay. The two exceptions, which apply to civil as well as to criminal proceedings, are these: to prove an act done by, or the state of mind at the time of his act of a person, evidence is not admissible: (1) of similar acts done by himself, if they do no more than show a general disposition, habit or propensity to commit such acts and a consequent probability of his having committed the act, or possessed the state of mind in question (See however Lawry v. R. (17-21 post), where the Privy Council appear to have held that evidence of general disposition is admissible by one co-defendant in a criminal case against another), and (2) of similar acts done by others, similarly circumstanced to himself, to show that he would be likely to act as they did (Brown v. Eastern & Midlands Ry. Co. (1889), 22 Q.B.D. 391, per Stephen, J.). If, however, evidence of similar acts done by the person whose act or state of mind is in question is such that it might lead a reasonable jury to the conclusion that the similarity could not be explained by coincidence, or conspiracy by the witnesses to make similar false allegations, or repetition as facts of things read or heard, e.g., on television, the evidence is admissible on the basis that the probative force of two or more such similar acts is greater than of one alone (See § § 17-43 et seq., post). Thus, in certain circumstances the similar fact exception will apply and evidence of past bad acts will be admissible. This is limited to cases where the past bad acts are so similar in nature to the acts now alleged that the latter can be found to be part of the defendant's modus operandi, scheme or system of acting, sufficient to constitute a hallmark or signature of his conduct, and sufficiently similar to dispel any concern than the similarity might be due to coincidence. The Supreme Court of Canada recently pronounced on similar fact principles, and held that the strictness of the test for admissibility depends on what the similar facts are intended to prove. Where, for example, identity is being proved, a standard approaching “striking similarity” of the facts is required, whereas if the similar fact evidence is adduced to prove a fact in issue the standard is less rigorous. In all instances, however, there must be sufficient similarity to ensure that it is unlikely that the similarity is the product of coincidence, i.e., that there is an “objective improbability of coincidence”. In R. v. Arp (B.) (1998), 232 N.R. 317 (S.C.C.), Cory, J., addresses the similar facts test in the criminal context (the following are excerpts, not a complete quotation of his Lordship's relevant rules, from 316, 317 and 319): Because similar fact evidence is admitted on the basis of an objective improbability of coincidence, the evidence necessarily derives its probative value from the degree of similarity between the acts under consideration. The probative value must, of course, significantly outweigh the prejudice to the accused for the evidence to be admissible. See B.(C.R.), [[1990] 1 S.C.R. 717]. However, the majority in B.(C.R.), at pp. 732-733, rejected the proposition that the evidence must show a ‘striking similarity’ between the acts in question in order for the evidence to have the requisite probative value. I agree that the requirement of ‘striking similarity’ needs to be qualified. … Instead, a principled approach to the admission of similar fact evidence will in all cases rest on the finding that the accused's involvement in the alleged similar acts or counts is unlikely to be the product of coincidence. This conclusion ensures that the evidence has sufficient probative force to be admitted, and will involve different considerations in different contexts. Where, as here, similar fact evidence is adduced on the issue of identity, there must be a high degree of similarity between the acts for the evidence to be admitted. For example, a unique trade mark or signature will automatically render the alleged acts ‘strikingly similar’ and therefore highly probative and admissible. In the same way, a number of significant similarities, taken together, may be such that by their cumulative effect, they warrant admission of the evidence. Where identity is at issue ordinarily, the trial judge should review the manner in which the similar acts were committed—that is to say, whether the similar acts involve a unique trade mark or reveal a number of significant similarities. … Thus, where similar fact evidence is adduced to prove a fact in issue, in order to be admissible, the trial judge should evaluate the degree of similarity of the alleged acts and decide whether the objective improbability of coincidence has been established. Only then will the evidence have sufficient probative value to be admitted… ..... Arp dealt with a double first degree murder and the proper charge to a jury in respect of using similar fact evidence to prove identity. That situation requires as high a degree of similarity as will ever be required in the courts, but I believe that Arp is nevertheless relevant to the civil context because, in my view, it is also appropriate civilly to require a higher degree of similarity when proving the identity of a defendant than when simply proving a fact in issue. The primary difference between civil and criminal cases, as regards similar fact evidence, is that it is appropriate in the criminal context to be vigilant to ensure that the evidence's prejudicial effect does not outweigh its probative value. This difference is addressed in an excerpt from Cross and Tapper on Evidence (8th Ed.) (London: Butterworths, 1995). The authors first note that there is no reason in principle that similar fact evidence should not apply to civil cases, but that in civil cases the primary question is essentially one of relevance. Once relevance is established, the evidence should only be excluded according to a rule based on a relaxed criminal standard, which, according to the primary English authority, is that it would not be “oppressive or unfair” to the other side to admit it. I agree with that relaxed standard since it represents a reasonable balancing of the parties' competing interests and is appropriate to civil matters where the court need not be as sensitive to potential “prejudice” as it must be in the criminal arena (at pp. 410-411): Although some early civil cases [citations omitted] rejected similar fact evidence as res inter alios acta [forbidden use of collateral facts which by their nature are incapable of providing any reasonable presumption or inference to a matter in dispute], it was soon accepted that the rule of exclusion was certainly no stricter than in criminal cases [citations omitted]… In more recent times there has been a further relaxation of the exclusionary rules in civil cases, and Lord Reid doubted whether the same considerations which justified the rule in criminal cases applied in the civil law (Cummings (McWilliams v. Sir William Arrol & Co., [1962] 1 All E.R. 623 at p. 630 …). The most authoritative recent statement of the position was made by Lord Denning, M.R., in Mood Music Publishing Co Ltd v. de Wolfe, [[1976] 1 All E.R. 763 (C.A.)] The plaintiffs in an action for infringement of copyright wished to tender evidence of previous infringements of copyright by the defendant. The trial judge decided the question of admissibility on considerations of ordinary relevance without reference to any special exclusionary rule. In this he was upheld by the Court of Appeal, on the basis that no more than such relevance was required in civil cases by contrast with criminal cases [at p. 766]: The criminal courts have been very careful not to admit such evidence unless its probative value is so strong that it should be received in the interests of justice; and its admission will not operate unfairly to the accused. In civil cases the courts will admit evidence of similar facts if it is logically probative, that is if it is logically relevant in determining the matter which is in issue; provided that it is not oppressive or unfair to the other side; and also that the other side has fair notice of it and is able to deal with it. . . . . . Once relevance is established using similar fact rules, we have a choice of two principles for determining whether such relevant evidence should nevertheless be excluded. The criminal exclusionary rule is that a relevant similar fact document's probative value must significantly outweigh any prejudice to the defendant, whereas the civil exclusionary rule is that a relevant similar fact document should be admitted unless to do so would be oppressive or unfair. For reasons set out above as regards the different weighting of probity versus prejudice in civil versus criminal courts, I believe that the correct standard for civil courts is the civil standard. Moreover, I question whether using a criminal exclusionary rule actually adds anything to the test set out by Lord Denning in Mood Music Publishing. A trial judge sitting with a civil jury will of course determine oppressiveness and unfairness while cognizant that a jury is the trier of fact and that juries may be less sophisticated than judges when weighing similar fact evidence. Given that control or buffer against oppression or unfairness, I believe Lord Denning's approach is sufficient, so see no reason to depart from his ruling in Mood Music Publishing. And finally, I note that in Arp the Supreme Court of Canada held that, as between the two standards of proof, beyond a reasonable doubt and on a balance of probabilities, a jury should be instructed to apply the civil standard when determining, in a multi-count indictment, whether the same person committed the acts (paragraphs 58-75, at pp. 323-329). It seems appropriate by analogy, albeit for a different purpose here, that once relevance is proved according to the contextual approach in Arp that Lord Denning's civil standard of exclusion be applied rather than [the] criminal standard. To conclude this Part, I take two principles from Arp and Mood Music Publishing: a) Arp: The degree of similarity required for admissibility depends upon what the similar facts are intended to prove, with, for example, proof of identity requiring similarity approaching “striking similarity” whereas proof of a fact in issue requires only that there is an objective improbability of coincidence. This contextual approach to determining relevance for admissibility is, in my view, appropriate in the civil context as well, although the continuum in the civil arena may not require as high a degree of similarity at the upper end of the spectrum as do criminal courts. b) Mood Music Publishing: In civil cases, once relevance has been established according to the contextual approach outlined in Arp, the evidence should be admitted unless it falls foul of a relaxed criminal standard of prejudice, that is instead of excluding relevant evidence because its probative value fails to significantly outweigh the prejudice it may cause, it should be admitted unless it would be unfair or oppressive to the other side. Whereas the criminal courts are more concerned with prejudice than probity, civil courts are more concerned with probity and relevance than with prejudice, so it is appropriate that the latter apply a more relaxed or tolerant standard of exclusion. . . . . . …[Thorpe v. Chief Constable of Greater Manchester, [1989] 2 All E.R. 827 (C.A.)] is a useful case which sets out the following principles for the discoverability of documents alleged to be relevant based on similar fact principles. Following the Phipson on Evidence (supra) approach, namely that all relevant documents should be admitted unless these show no more than a propensity to be a bad actor, Dillon, L.J., sets out the general rule relating to discovery of documents and then qualifies it with a series of exceptions relevant to discovery based on similar fact rules. Counsel in this Application agreed that the following general discovery principle stated by Dillon, L.J., represents the law in Alberta (at p. 829): Discovery is to be given [under the Rules of Court] of all documents ‘relating to any matter in question’ between the parties in the action. It is very well established, however, as explained in [the Rules] that the words ‘relating to any matter in question between them [the parties]’ refer not to the subject matter of an action but to the questions in the action, and that any document must be disclosed which it is reasonable to suppose contains information which may enable the party applying for discovery either to advance his own case or to damage that of his adversary or which may fairly lead him to a train of inquiry which may have either of these two consequences. Discovery is thus not necessarily limited to documents which would be admissible in evidence. Dillon, L.J., starting at p. 829, then describes the exceptions to this general rule when dealing with discovery based on similar facts principles: The first is that the court should not order discovery, or interrogatories, which are a form of discovery, of matters which would go solely to cross-examination as to credit… It would indeed be an impossible situation in my view if discovery had to be given of every document, not relevant to the actual issues in the action, which might open up a line of inquiry for cross-examination of the litigant solely as to credit. In the second place, while … there are cases in which the evidence of what happened in one transaction may be relevant to the question of what happened in another, where that is not so to order discovery in respect of what may turn out to be similar fact transactions would likely to be oppressive and so the order should not be made. That is very much emphasized in the judgments of Lord Herschell, L.C. and Lindley, L.J., in Kennedy v Dodson, [[1895] 1 Ch 334 (C.A.)] That fully justifies the decision in George Ballantine & Son Ltd. v. F E R Dixon & Son Ltd., [[1974] 2 All E.R. 503], where the plaintiffs in their pleading alleged passing off by the defendant in the supply of whisky in named countries, and sought discovery of documents relating to the defendant's supply of whisky, and it would seem gin, to other countries. ..... Returning to his Lordship's list of “relevant limitations” on the general principle of similar fact discoverability of documents, Lord Dillon comes to what is perhaps the largest of his exceptions (at p. 830): The reconciliation between this principle [to disallow similar fact evidence which merely proves a propensity or disposition to act in a certain way] and the rule in the [Rules of Court] that there should be discovery of documents which may fairly lead the applicant for discovery to a train of inquiry which may advance the litigant's own case or damage that of his adversary is, in my judgment, that a train of inquiry which can only lead to matters which would not be admissible in evidence (save solely in cross-examination as to credit) does not lead to either of those two desirable ends. (emphasis added) In other words, even though the ordinary discovery rule is to sometimes allow, on the basis of the “train of inquiry” principle, documents which might not ultimately be admissible at trial, that principle cannot apply in cases of similar fact documents which can only lead to proof of something which would not be admissible in evidence at trial. In such cases, since permitting discovery of those documents serves no policy objective, nor in my view does it lead to a legitimate “train of inquiry”, his Lordship held that such documents should be found not discoverable. This final exclusionary principle addresses the rather important question raised above, namely, in the context of discovery of documents, what is the correct threshold of relevance and therefore discoverability when that relevance is based on similar fact principles—the usual generous “train of inquiry” rule, or the more stringent “admissibility at trial” rule. I agree with Dillon, L.J., that the correct test for determining discoverability of similar fact documents is the admissibility at trial rule notwithstanding that this is a determination made in the context of discovery. Mr Rolf, on behalf of the applicant Nelson, made a submission with which I had some fleeting sympathy—that without access to the RCMP and Prosecutors' Documents he is prevented from reviewing documents which may fairly lead him to a train of inquiry which could be used to strengthen his case or weaken that of the respondents. He is, effectively, forced to work in the dark. This is not, however, an ordinary application for discovery. The relevance of the documents here is predicated on the similar fact rule. It is not sufficient, in my view, to simply allege that the documents may be relevant because they may qualify under the similar fact rule. That is what the court held in Thorpe. It also begs the question on the very issue which determines this Application—relevance—because it attempts to apply a general discovery principle to bypass a more specific and rigorous test required to prove relevance in cases of similar fact evidence. If a sufficient evidentiary foundation had been advanced, and had this established sufficient similarity between the past and current conducts alleged against Young, Mr. Rolf would have been given access, barring issues of control and privilege, to the relevant documents. Put simply, the rule is that one may discover only relevant documents, and if the sole reason for the documents' alleged relevance is based on similar fact principles, then one must, to meet the relevancy threshold for discovery, pass the test required for the admission of similar fact evidence. It is not appropriate, in my view, given the high policy reasons for requiring similar fact evidence to go through a rigorous relevance test—namely to prevent findings of liability based on mere habit, propensity or disposition—to lower the threshold simply because the request arises in the context of discovery. Nor, to anticipate an argument not made in this Application, is it acceptable to lower the threshold at discovery on the basis that there remains the safety-net that the trial judge will not ultimately admit that evidence unless it passes the stricter admissibility test, for that would be establishing a rule which permitted discovery of documents which were not relevant. In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2013 ABQB 439, 2013 CarswellAlta 1501, 558 A.R. 361, 88 Alta. L.R. (5th) 149, the Plaintiff sued the defendant in relation to allegedly defective pipe which had been supplied to the Plaintiff by the Defendant. In an application to compel production of certain records, Madam Justice Hughes discussed “similar fact evidence”. At paragraphs 28–41, her Ladyship said: 28 In the text by Lawrence G. Theall et al, Product Liability: Canadian Law and Practice, loose leaf (consulted on 30 July 2013), (Aurora, ON: Canada Law Book, 2012) the authors observe at p. P2–11: … courts generally consider information relating to prior incidents involving the same product relevant to the issues of whether the product or model had inherent defects, and the defendant's awareness of the same [notes omitted]. 29 In the above emails, redactions were made. The clear inference from the emails is that the redacted information deals with problems relating to other A106 Grade B pipe, which is the same type of pipe as the Subject Pipe, but which fall outside the definition of relevance the Defendants have taken. 30 The authors discuss the issue of similar fact evidence in a product liability case at p. L8-15–17: As with evidence that a defendant took remedial measures following a plaintiff's injury, evidence of other accidents or occurrences similar to the plaintiff's can prove troublesome for the defendant and useful for the plaintiff in a product liability case. The plaintiff may wish to introduce the evidence to establish a number of facts, including the defendant's habitual negligence and the existence of a defect or unsafe condition. Almost always, the defendant will have a keen interest in keeping evidence of other accidents or defects involving its products out of trial for fear that it will prejudice the trier of fact against the defendant's case. Evidence of a past defect or negligence might lead the judge or jury to wrongly assume that a defect or negligence must also exist in the present case. As will be seen, admissibility of this evidence depends primarily on whether the evidence would be oppressive or unfair to the defendant. … In determining whether to allow similar fact evidence, courts have developed separate tests for criminal and civil cases. In criminal matters, similar fact evidence is not admissible unless its probative value is so strong that the evidence should be received in the interests of justice. Even so, courts will reject the evidence if its admission would operate unfairly against the accused. The test for admissibility is not nearly as stringent in civil litigation. As long as the similar fact evidence is logically probative, courts will receive the evidence unless its admission would be unfair or oppressive to the other party. Courts generally require fair notice to the other party to allow sufficient time to prepare to met the evidence. … The categories of cases where similar fact evidence will be permitted are not closed. Courts appear to admit the evidence whenever a real and substantial nexus exists between an act or allegation in the case and the facts surrounding the similar event or transaction. … In product liability claims, plaintiffs often seek the admission of similar fact evidence to prove one of two conditions: the propensities of a manufactured product; or the state or condition of premises [notes omitted]. 31 The authors also observe at p. P2-10-11: Similar fact evidence can take many forms in a product liability case. This information may include such things as reports of customer contacts or complaints regarding the product, reports on product quality issued by dealers and retailers, and field investigation reports. Chapter L8, “Common Evidentiary Issues in Product Cases”, considers the admissibility of similar fact evidence at trial. Although the same principles are relevant to the question of whether similar fact evidence can form a proper basis for discovery requests, given the broad scope of discovery, courts have developed additional principles for resolving this issue. In many cases, the plaintiff will be permitted to obtain discovery of information about prior incidents, even though the evidence may ultimately be held inadmissible at trial. Although the scope of discovery is very broad throughout Canada, the information sought must be relevant to the case, in the sense that the information must at least relate to a matter in issue. Relevance for discovery purposes is determined by the pleadings in the case … 32 Simply put, similar fact evidence is circumstantial evidence from which a trier of fact is asked to draw certain inferences and make findings of fact. This was clearly articulated in R. v. Batte (2000), 49 OR (3d) 321 at para 97, 145 CCC (3d) 449 (ONCA), albeit in the criminal law context in relation to bad character evidence: Propensity reasoning involves two inferences. First, one infers from conduct on occasions other than the occasion in issue that a person has a certain disposition (state of mind). Second, one infers from the existence of that disposition that a person acted in a certain way on the occasion in issue … Assuming the evidence can reasonably support both inferences, there is nothing irrational or illogical in using propensity reasoning to infer that an accused committed the act alleged. Viewed in this way, the evidence of the accused's discreditable conduct is a form of circumstantial evidence and meets the legal relevance criterion [notes omitted]. 33 This same rationale was articulated with respect to a product liability case by Wachowich A.C.J. (as he then was) in KN v. Alberta, 1999 ABQB 270 at para. 23, 243 AR 94: With manufactured products, if something is wrong with a machine causing it to produce defective widgets, transmissions or Cessnas, if the plaintiff's same widget, transmission or Cessna is defective in the same way, then other instances of similarly defective products produced by the same machine are highly relevant and probative, as there is a substantial likelihood that the defect in the product was produced by the defective machine. Human behaviour is, fortunately, not so predictable or immutable. 34 In Trans-Border Plastics Ltd v. Leavens Air Charter Ltd (1982), 36 OR (2d) 731 at 735, [1982] O.J. No. 2565 (ON HCJ) [“Trans-Border Plastics”], the purchaser of a faulty Cessna airplane applied for an order requiring the defendant to produce “airplane condition reports possessed by Cessna in relation to all 421C aircraft and relating to conditions complained of in the action.” This included any reports on any 421C aircraft made at any time, which the defendant claimed was unnecessarily onerous and, therefore, subject to exclusion under the similar fact rule. The Court stated at p. 735-36: … if defects of the nature complained of by the plaintiff are prevalent in other aircraft of the same model and manufactured pursuant to the same plans such evidence is relevant in the determination of the issue of whether the 421C aircraft has inherent defects. Whether such evidence is admissible at the trial will be determined by the trial judge. I am, however, persuaded by the decisions of the Alberta and British Columbia Courts that information concerning defects in other machines or in the component parts is relevant and such information should be disclosed at the discovery stage. 35 The Alberta decision referred to was Tachit v. Versatile Mfg Ltd (1978), 11 AR 544 [“Tachit”]. In this case, the plaintiff claimed negligence in the manufacture of a tractor and sought any information regarding transmission problems in other similar tractors. McFadyen J. found this was relevant, and cited MacDonald J. in Busslinger v. Bow Valley Machinery (Calgary) Ltd, [1975] A.J. No. 57, (6 February 1975) Calgary 101405 (AB Sup Ct) [“Busslinger”], as follows: … it is relevant in this case, when the defectiveness of a machine and whether or not there was negligence in its manufacture, assembly, distribution or sale is in issue, that the plaintiff seek the defendants' information as to the quality of the machine in question gained as a result of the tests that may have been conducted or similar things manufactured, assembled or distributed or sold by the defendants, and of the results of inspection of similar things, whether or not in any particular case such information is gained subsequent to the event in issue or not. 36 The Trans-Border Plastics, Tachit, and Busslinger cases are all “product liability” cases. Although the cases predate the current wording of Rule 5.2, all dealt with the question of what is relevant at discovery, and all found the information at issue to be relevant and producible. I find the information in these cases falls within today's definition of secondary relevance because the information ordered produced, was information from which the existence of primary facts could be directly inferred. 37 The Defendants have characterized the information being sought in this application as a search for tertiary or “similar fact evidence.” As such, they argue, it is inadmissible. 38 I agree with the Defendants that similar fact evidence is presumptively inadmissible. See R. v. Handy, 2002 SCC 56, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 908. That however does not make the information sought not relevant. See for example R. v. Batte, supra. A number of other evidentiary principles must also be remembered. First, evidence that is presumptively inadmissible for one purpose may be admissible for another purpose; see for example Cheyne v. Alberta, 2003 ABQB 244. Second, the admissibility of evidence is dependant on the context of the other trial evidence. Therefore to my mind, the determination of admissibility of evidence is a function of the trial judge. It is not the function of the case management judge: see TW v. University of Alberta Hospital, 2000 ABQB 387 at para 28, 267 AR 169. 39 One of the issues at trial will be whether the Subject Pipe was negligently manufactured; that makes this a “product liability” case. Thus, if defects of the nature complained of by CNRL are prevalent in other A106 Grade B pipe manufactured by Mittal at its Roman Mill, such evidence may well be relevant in determining whether the Subject Pipe was negligently manufactured. 40 From the evidence before me it is clear that Vass notified Mittal of five other quality incidents. Other emails refer to “quality concerns”, materials shipped prior to July, 2005 as “unsure”, and corrective measures being implemented. Mr. Goel testified Mittal had retained Bureau Veritas on June 29, 2005 for its third party inspection of material for North America. Those inspections began August 2005. 41 If there were manufacturing issues and/or inherent defects respecting the A106 Grade B pipe manufactured by Mittal at the Roman Mill during the same time-frame as that when the Subject Pipe was being made, this is evidence which could give rise to a very strong inference regarding the manner of the pipe's manufacture which could significantly help determine the negligence and breach of contract issues raised in CNRL's Statements of Claim, and as such it would qualify as “secondary” evidence as described by the Court of Appeal in NAC Constructors. Therefore, I find the information sought by CNRL is relevant. In Kaddoura v. Hanson, 2015 ABCA 154, the Court dealt with two consolidated appeals which involved alleged mortgage fraud schemes. The alleged scheme was alleged to work as follows: a fraudulent person (“the fraudster”) would agree to purchase a piece of land from the original owner at a fair market price. The fraudster would then recruit a “straw buyer” who would agreed to purchase the land from the fraudster at an inflated value. The property would then be transferred directly from the original owner to the straw buyer. A financial institution would be induced to lend money and take a mortgage the amount of which would be based on the inflated value. The money in excess of the original sale price would then be pocketed by the fraudster after the straw buyer is paid a fee for participating. In the consolidated appeals before the Court of Appeal, the Royal Bank had been granted mortgages by persons alleged to be straw buyers. When the mortgages went into default, the Bank commenced actions for the shortfalls against the alleged straw buyers (in whose names the properties were registered and who had granted the mortgages to the Bank), and the straw buyers then sued (or third partied) the lawyer who had represented the parties in the transactions. The matter before the Court of Appeal related to the lawyer's appeal of a Master's order which required the lawyer to disclose the existence of certain documents on other files in which the lawyer had acted for the alleged fraudster. The Court said: 11 The respondents' proposed line of argument is that if the lawyer was involved in numerous other files involving the same main fraudster, it would support an inference that the lawyer actually knew, or “ought to have known” that something illegitimate was going on. In other words, the straw buyers seek to use circumstantial evidence to prove the state of mind or state of knowledge of the lawyers. Irregularities in any one real estate file may simply be an aberration; a pattern of files with similar irregularities arguably calls for an explanation. In order to support this line of argument, the straw buyers seek production of other client files in the lawyer's offices involving the same alleged main fraudster or bank loans officer. The argument is that if those files disclose a pattern of irregularities, it will assist the straw buyers in proving one of the issues in the litigation. 12 The plaintiffs essentially seek “similar fact evidence” in the discovery process. While that sort of evidence is more common in criminal cases, it can be used in civil cases as well. Mood Music Publishing Co. v De Wolfe Ltd., [1976] Ch 119, [1976] 1 All ER 763 (CA), concerned allegations of breach of copyright. The defendant pleaded that any similarity between its published work and that of the plaintiff was mere coincidence. The plaintiff was permitted to use evidence of other breaches of copyright by the defendant in order to show a pattern of conduct. The evidence was circumstantial evidence of the defendant's knowledge and intent. 13 This type of evidence was also used in Greenglass v Rusonik, [1983] OJ No 40 (CA), an action against solicitors over a complex real estate transaction. An inflated sale price was one feature of the scheme. Evidence that the defendant solicitors had participated in other similar transactions was admitted “to show system, state of mind, knowledge and intent” (at para. 48). If that sort of evidence can potentially be probative at trial, there is no reason in principle why it cannot be explored during the discovery process. 14 At the production stage of the litigation, it is not necessary to decide whether the trial judge will or will not be prepared to draw the inferences from the circumstantial evidence put forward by the respondents. Nor must the respondents demonstrate conclusively that the discovered records will in fact contain any evidence of assistance to them. It may be that the client files will be produced, be examined, and be shown to have no probative value under any theory of the case. However, at this stage of the litigation the respondents need only show a plausible line of argument: Dow Chemical Canada ULC v Nova Chemicals Corp., 2014 ABCA 244 at para. 21, 577 AR 335; Weatherill (Estate) v Weatherill, 2003 ABQB 69 at para. 16, 11 Alta LR (4th) 183, 337 AR 180.

sentences.text: 7.2-13 A lawyer who comes into possession of a privileged communication of an opposing party must not make use of it and must immediately advise the opposing lawyer or opposing party.

The Commentary to the Code of Conduct continues: [2] Immediately upon realizing that the communication is a privileged communication of another party, the lawyer shall not continue to read the communication and must bring it to the attention of opposing counsel, then return or destroy it, without copies having been made.

Knowledge that a communication is not intended for the lawyer receiving it will be imputed if, under the circumstances, it would have been unreasonable for the lawyer to come to any other conclusion. … [4] In the event there is a genuine dispute over the nature of the communication, it shall be permissible for the receiving lawyer to secure the communication, pending resolution of the dispute.
The issue of whether or to what extent the communication may be copied or its contents disclosed or used must be resolved by agreement or by the court.
In the meantime, it is improper to use the communication or disclose its contents in any manner.

Alberta (1999), 243 A.R.
94 (Q.B.), the plaintiff in a wrongful sexual sterilization action against the Province of Alberta sought production of certain records on the basis that they contained similar fact evidence.
Wachowich A.C.J.Q.B. held that the concept of similar fact evidence applied to civil proceedings, but that the test differed from that used in the criminal law.
As there is little law in Alberta on this topic, his Lordship's detailed analysis is worth repeating.
At pp.

98-107, his Lordship said: The admissibility of similar fact evidence is an exception to the general exclusionary rule of evidence which prohibits a party from adducing evidence of the bad character of the opposite party to prove or disprove a fact in issue.

Put simply, the exclusionary rule is that it is insufficient and dangerous to determine civil or criminal liability on no more than a person's general disposition, habit or propensity to be a bad actor… Stated another way, which is perhaps the best way of approaching similar fact evidence in the context of discovery where relevance is the primary criterion, Phipson on Evidence (14th Ed.) (London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1990) begins with the principle that everything relevant should be admitted, and then subjects that rule to two exceptions, excluding relevant information where this would prove no more than a propensity to be a bad actor or to act like other bad actors in similar circumstances (at p.

373): Subject to two exceptions stated below, evidence of facts or transactions similar to the fact or transaction directly in issue is admissible if it is logically probative, that is if it is logically relevant in determining the matter which is in issue (Per Lord Denning, M.R., in Mood Music Publishing Co.
Ltd. v. de Wolfe Ltd., [1976] 2 W.L.R.
451, 456 (C.A.)), and it is not otherwise excluded, e.g., by the rule against hearsay.
The two exceptions, which apply to civil as well as to criminal proceedings, are these: to prove an act done by, or the state of mind at the time of his act of a person, evidence is not admissible:

(1) of similar acts done by himself, if they do no more than show a general disposition, habit or propensity to commit such acts and a consequent probability of his having committed the act, or possessed the state of mind in question (See however Lawry v.
R.
(17-21 post), where the Privy Council appear to have held that evidence of general disposition is admissible by one co-defendant in a criminal case against another), and
(2) of similar acts done by others, similarly circumstanced to himself, to show that he would be likely to act as they did (Brown v.
Eastern & Midlands Ry.
Co.
391, per Stephen, J.).

If, however, evidence of similar acts done by the person whose act or state of mind is in question is such that it might lead a reasonable jury to the conclusion that the similarity could not be explained by coincidence, or conspiracy by the witnesses to make similar false allegations, or repetition as facts of things read or heard, e.g., on television, the evidence is admissible on the basis that the probative force of two or more such similar acts is greater than of one alone (See § § 17-43 et seq., post).
Thus, in certain circumstances the similar fact exception will apply and evidence of past bad acts will be admissible.

This is limited to cases where the past bad acts are so similar in nature to the acts now alleged that the latter can be found to be part of the defendant's modus operandi, scheme or system of acting, sufficient to constitute a hallmark or signature of his conduct, and sufficiently similar to dispel any concern than the similarity might be due to coincidence.
The Supreme Court of Canada recently pronounced on similar fact principles, and held that the strictness of the test for admissibility depends on what the similar facts are intended to prove.

Where, for example, identity is being proved, a standard approaching “striking similarity” of the facts is required, whereas if the similar fact evidence is adduced to prove a fact in issue the standard is less rigorous.

In all instances, however, there must be sufficient similarity to ensure that it is unlikely that the similarity is the product of coincidence, i.e., that there is an “objective improbability of coincidence”.
In R. v.

317 (S.C.C.), Cory, J., addresses the similar facts test in the criminal context (the following are excerpts, not a complete quotation of his Lordship's relevant rules, from 316, 317 and 319): Because similar fact evidence is admitted on the basis of an objective improbability of coincidence, the evidence necessarily derives its probative value from the degree of similarity between the acts under consideration.
The probative value must, of course, significantly outweigh the prejudice to the accused for the evidence to be admissible.
However, the majority in B.(C.R.), at pp.
732-733, rejected the proposition that the evidence must show a ‘striking similarity’ between the acts in question in order for the evidence to have the requisite probative value.

I agree that the requirement of ‘striking similarity’ needs to be qualified. … Instead, a principled approach to the admission of similar fact evidence will in all cases rest on the finding that the accused's involvement in the alleged similar acts or counts is unlikely to be the product of coincidence.
This conclusion ensures that the evidence has sufficient probative force to be admitted, and will involve different considerations in different contexts.
Where, as here, similar fact evidence is adduced on the issue of identity, there must be a high degree of similarity between the acts for the evidence to be admitted.
For example, a unique trade mark or signature will automatically render the alleged acts ‘strikingly similar’ and therefore highly probative and admissible.
In the same way, a number of significant similarities, taken together, may be such that by their cumulative effect, they warrant admission of the evidence.

Where identity is at issue ordinarily, the trial judge should review the manner in which the similar acts were committed—that is to say, whether the similar acts involve a unique trade mark or reveal a number of significant similarities. … Thus, where similar fact evidence is adduced to prove a fact in issue, in order to be admissible, the trial judge should evaluate the degree of similarity of the alleged acts and decide whether the objective improbability of coincidence has been established.
Only then will the evidence have sufficient probative value to be admitted… .....
Arp dealt with a double first degree murder and the proper charge to a jury in respect of using similar fact evidence to prove identity.

That situation requires as high a degree of similarity as will ever be required in the courts, but I believe that Arp is nevertheless relevant to the civil context because, in my view, it is also appropriate civilly to require a higher degree of similarity when proving the identity of a defendant than when simply proving a fact in issue.

The primary difference between civil and criminal cases, as regards similar fact evidence, is that it is appropriate in the criminal context to be vigilant to ensure that the evidence's prejudicial effect does not outweigh its probative value.
This difference is addressed in an excerpt from Cross and Tapper on Evidence (8th Ed.) (London: Butterworths, 1995).
The authors first note that there is no reason in principle that similar fact evidence should not apply to civil cases, but that in civil cases the primary question is essentially one of relevance.

Once relevance is established, the evidence should only be excluded according to a rule based on a relaxed criminal standard, which, according to the primary English authority, is that it would not be “oppressive or unfair” to the other side to admit it.

I agree with that relaxed standard since it represents a reasonable balancing of the parties' competing interests and is appropriate to civil matters where the court need not be as sensitive to potential “prejudice” as it must be in the criminal arena (at pp.

410-411): Although some early civil cases [citations omitted] rejected similar fact evidence as res inter alios acta [forbidden use of collateral facts which by their nature are incapable of providing any reasonable presumption or inference to a matter in dispute], it was soon accepted that the rule of exclusion was certainly no stricter than in criminal cases [citations omitted]… In more recent times there has been a further relaxation of the exclusionary rules in civil cases, and Lord Reid doubted whether the same considerations which justified the rule in criminal cases applied in the civil law (Cummings (McWilliams v.
Sir William Arrol & Co., [1962] 1 All E.R.
623 at p.
The most authoritative recent statement of the position was made by Lord Denning, M.R., in Mood Music Publishing Co Ltd v. de Wolfe, [[1976] 1 All E.R.
763 (C.A.)] The plaintiffs in an action for infringement of copyright wished to tender evidence of previous infringements of copyright by the defendant.
The trial judge decided the question of admissibility on considerations of ordinary relevance without reference to any special exclusionary rule.
In this he was upheld by the Court of Appeal, on the basis that no more than such relevance was required in civil cases by contrast with criminal cases [at p.

766]: The criminal courts have been very careful not to admit such evidence unless its probative value is so strong that it should be received in the interests of justice; and its admission will not operate unfairly to the accused.

In civil cases the courts will admit evidence of similar facts if it is logically probative, that is if it is logically relevant in determining the matter which is in issue; provided that it is not oppressive or unfair to the other side; and also that the other side has fair notice of it and is able to deal with it. . . . . .
Once relevance is established using similar fact rules, we have a choice of two principles for determining whether such relevant evidence should nevertheless be excluded.

The criminal exclusionary rule is that a relevant similar fact document's probative value must significantly outweigh any prejudice to the defendant, whereas the civil exclusionary rule is that a relevant similar fact document should be admitted unless to do so would be oppressive or unfair.
For reasons set out above as regards the different weighting of probity versus prejudice in civil versus criminal courts, I believe that the correct standard for civil courts is the civil standard.
Moreover, I question whether using a criminal exclusionary rule actually adds anything to the test set out by Lord Denning in Mood Music Publishing.

A trial judge sitting with a civil jury will of course determine oppressiveness and unfairness while cognizant that a jury is the trier of fact and that juries may be less sophisticated than judges when weighing similar fact evidence.
Given that control or buffer against oppression or unfairness, I believe Lord Denning's approach is sufficient, so see no reason to depart from his ruling in Mood Music Publishing.

And finally, I note that in Arp the Supreme Court of Canada held that, as between the two standards of proof, beyond a reasonable doubt and on a balance of probabilities, a jury should be instructed to apply the civil standard when determining, in a multi-count indictment, whether the same person committed the acts (paragraphs 58-75, at pp.

It seems appropriate by analogy, albeit for a different purpose here, that once relevance is proved according to the contextual approach in Arp that Lord Denning's civil standard of exclusion be applied rather than [the] criminal standard.

To conclude this Part, I take two principles from Arp and Mood Music Publishing: a) Arp: The degree of similarity required for admissibility depends upon what the similar facts are intended to prove, with, for example, proof of identity requiring similarity approaching “striking similarity” whereas proof of a fact in issue requires only that there is an objective improbability of coincidence.

This contextual approach to determining relevance for admissibility is, in my view, appropriate in the civil context as well, although the continuum in the civil arena may not require as high a degree of similarity at the upper end of the spectrum as do criminal courts. b) Mood Music Publishing: In civil cases, once relevance has been established according to the contextual approach outlined in Arp, the evidence should be admitted unless it falls foul of a relaxed criminal standard of prejudice, that is instead of excluding relevant evidence because its probative value fails to significantly outweigh the prejudice it may cause, it should be admitted unless it would be unfair or oppressive to the other side.

Whereas the criminal courts are more concerned with prejudice than probity, civil courts are more concerned with probity and relevance than with prejudice, so it is appropriate that the latter apply a more relaxed or tolerant standard of exclusion. . . . . . …[Thorpe v.
Chief Constable of Greater Manchester, [1989] 2 All E.R.
827 (C.A.)] is a useful case which sets out the following principles for the discoverability of documents alleged to be relevant based on similar fact principles.
Following the Phipson on Evidence

(supra) approach, namely that all relevant documents should be admitted unless these show no more than a propensity to be a bad actor, Dillon, L.J., sets out the general rule relating to discovery of documents and then qualifies it with a series of exceptions relevant to discovery based on similar fact rules.
Counsel in this Application agreed that the following general discovery principle stated by Dillon, L.J., represents the law in Alberta (at p.
829): Discovery is to be given [under the Rules of Court] of all documents ‘relating to any matter in question’ between the parties in the action.

It is very well established, however, as explained in [the Rules] that the words ‘relating to any matter in question between them [the parties]’ refer not to the subject matter of an action but to the questions in the action, and that any document must be disclosed which it is reasonable to suppose contains information which may enable the party applying for discovery either to advance his own case or to damage that of his adversary or which may fairly lead him to a train of inquiry which may have either of these two consequences.
Discovery is thus not necessarily limited to documents which would be admissible in evidence.
Dillon, L.J., starting at p.

829, then describes the exceptions to this general rule when dealing with discovery based on similar facts principles: The first is that the court should not order discovery, or interrogatories, which are a form of discovery, of matters which would go solely to cross-examination as to credit… It would indeed be an impossible situation in my view if discovery had to be given of every document, not relevant to the actual issues in the action, which might open up a line of inquiry for cross-examination of the litigant solely as to credit.

In the second place, while … there are cases in which the evidence of what happened in one transaction may be relevant to the question of what happened in another, where that is not so to order discovery in respect of what may turn out to be similar fact transactions would likely to be oppressive and so the order should not be made.

That is very much emphasized in the judgments of Lord Herschell, L.C. and Lindley, L.J., in Kennedy v Dodson, [[1895] 1 Ch 334 (C.A.)] That fully justifies the decision in George Ballantine & Son Ltd. v.
F E R Dixon & Son Ltd., [[1974] 2 All E.R.

503], where the plaintiffs in their pleading alleged passing off by the defendant in the supply of whisky in named countries, and sought discovery of documents relating to the defendant's supply of whisky, and it would seem gin, to other countries. .....

Returning to his Lordship's list of “relevant limitations” on the general principle of similar fact discoverability of documents, Lord Dillon comes to what is perhaps the largest of his exceptions (at p.

830): The reconciliation between this principle [to disallow similar fact evidence which merely proves a propensity or disposition to act in a certain way] and the rule in the [Rules of Court] that there should be discovery of documents which may fairly lead the applicant for discovery to a train of inquiry which may advance the litigant's own case or damage that of his adversary is, in my judgment, that a train of inquiry which can only lead to matters which would not be admissible in evidence (save solely in cross-examination as to credit) does not lead to either of those two desirable ends.

(emphasis added) In other words, even though the ordinary discovery rule is to sometimes allow, on the basis of the “train of inquiry” principle, documents which might not ultimately be admissible at trial, that principle cannot apply in cases of similar fact documents which can only lead to proof of something which would not be admissible in evidence at trial.

In such cases, since permitting discovery of those documents serves no policy objective, nor in my view does it lead to a legitimate “train of inquiry”, his Lordship held that such documents should be found not discoverable.

This final exclusionary principle addresses the rather important question raised above, namely, in the context of discovery of documents, what is the correct threshold of relevance and therefore discoverability when that relevance is based on similar fact principles—the usual generous “train of inquiry” rule, or the more stringent “admissibility at trial” rule.

I agree with Dillon, L.J., that the correct test for determining discoverability of similar fact documents is the admissibility at trial rule notwithstanding that this is a determination made in the context of discovery.

Mr Rolf, on behalf of the applicant Nelson, made a submission with which I had some fleeting sympathy—that without access to the RCMP and Prosecutors' Documents he is prevented from reviewing documents which may fairly lead him to a train of inquiry which could be used to strengthen his case or weaken that of the respondents.
He is, effectively, forced to work in the dark.
This is not, however, an ordinary application for discovery.
The relevance of the documents here is predicated on the similar fact rule.
It is not sufficient, in my view, to simply allege that the documents may be relevant because they may qualify under the similar fact rule.
That is what the court held in Thorpe.

It also begs the question on the very issue which determines this Application—relevance—because it attempts to apply a general discovery principle to bypass a more specific and rigorous test required to prove relevance in cases of similar fact evidence.
If a sufficient evidentiary foundation had been advanced, and had this established sufficient similarity between the past and current conducts alleged against Young, Mr.
Rolf would have been given access, barring issues of control and privilege, to the relevant documents.

Put simply, the rule is that one may discover only relevant documents, and if the sole reason for the documents' alleged relevance is based on similar fact principles, then one must, to meet the relevancy threshold for discovery, pass the test required for the admission of similar fact evidence.

It is not appropriate, in my view, given the high policy reasons for requiring similar fact evidence to go through a rigorous relevance test—namely to prevent findings of liability based on mere habit, propensity or disposition—to lower the threshold simply because the request arises in the context of discovery.

Nor, to anticipate an argument not made in this Application, is it acceptable to lower the threshold at discovery on the basis that there remains the safety-net that the trial judge will not ultimately admit that evidence unless it passes the stricter admissibility test, for that would be establishing a rule which permitted discovery of documents which were not relevant.
In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v.
Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2013 ABQB 439, 2013 CarswellAlta 1501, 558 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 149, the Plaintiff sued the defendant in relation to allegedly defective pipe which had been supplied to the Plaintiff by the Defendant.
In an application to compel production of certain records, Madam Justice Hughes discussed “similar fact evidence”.
At paragraphs 28–41, her Ladyship said: 28 In the text by Lawrence G.
Theall et al, Product Liability: Canadian Law and Practice, loose leaf (consulted on 30 July 2013), (Aurora, ON: Canada Law Book, 2012) the authors observe at p.

P2–11: … courts generally consider information relating to prior incidents involving the same product relevant to the issues of whether the product or model had inherent defects, and the defendant's awareness of the same [notes omitted].
29 In the above emails, redactions were made.

The clear inference from the emails is that the redacted information deals with problems relating to other A106 Grade B pipe, which is the same type of pipe as the Subject Pipe, but which fall outside the definition of relevance the Defendants have taken.
30 The authors discuss the issue of similar fact evidence in a product liability case at p.

L8-15–17: As with evidence that a defendant took remedial measures following a plaintiff's injury, evidence of other accidents or occurrences similar to the plaintiff's can prove troublesome for the defendant and useful for the plaintiff in a product liability case.
The plaintiff may wish to introduce the evidence to establish a number of facts, including the defendant's habitual negligence and the existence of a defect or unsafe condition.

Almost always, the defendant will have a keen interest in keeping evidence of other accidents or defects involving its products out of trial for fear that it will prejudice the trier of fact against the defendant's case.
Evidence of a past defect or negligence might lead the judge or jury to wrongly assume that a defect or negligence must also exist in the present case.

As will be seen, admissibility of this evidence depends primarily on whether the evidence would be oppressive or unfair to the defendant. … In determining whether to allow similar fact evidence, courts have developed separate tests for criminal and civil cases.
In criminal matters, similar fact evidence is not admissible unless its probative value is so strong that the evidence should be received in the interests of justice.
Even so, courts will reject the evidence if its admission would operate unfairly against the accused.
The test for admissibility is not nearly as stringent in civil litigation.
As long as the similar fact evidence is logically probative, courts will receive the evidence unless its admission would be unfair or oppressive to the other party.

Courts generally require fair notice to the other party to allow sufficient time to prepare to met the evidence. … The categories of cases where similar fact evidence will be permitted are not closed.

Courts appear to admit the evidence whenever a real and substantial nexus exists between an act or allegation in the case and the facts surrounding the similar event or transaction. … In product liability claims, plaintiffs often seek the admission of similar fact evidence to prove one of two conditions: the propensities of a manufactured product; or the state or condition of premises [notes omitted].
31 The authors also observe at p.
P2-10-11: Similar fact evidence can take many forms in a product liability case.

This information may include such things as reports of customer contacts or complaints regarding the product, reports on product quality issued by dealers and retailers, and field investigation reports.
Chapter L8, “Common Evidentiary Issues in Product Cases”, considers the admissibility of similar fact evidence at trial.

Although the same principles are relevant to the question of whether similar fact evidence can form a proper basis for discovery requests, given the broad scope of discovery, courts have developed additional principles for resolving this issue.
In many cases, the plaintiff will be permitted to obtain discovery of information about prior incidents, even though the evidence may ultimately be held inadmissible at trial.
Although the scope of discovery is very broad throughout Canada, the information sought must be relevant to the case, in the sense that the information must at least relate to a matter in issue.

Relevance for discovery purposes is determined by the pleadings in the case … 32 Simply put, similar fact evidence is circumstantial evidence from which a trier of fact is asked to draw certain inferences and make findings of fact.
This was clearly articulated in R. v.
Batte (2000), 49 OR (3d) 321 at para 97, 145 CCC (3d) 449 (ONCA), albeit in the criminal law context in relation to bad character evidence: Propensity reasoning involves two inferences.
First, one infers from conduct on occasions other than the occasion in issue that a person has a certain disposition (state of mind).

Second, one infers from the existence of that disposition that a person acted in a certain way on the occasion in issue … Assuming the evidence can reasonably support both inferences, there is nothing irrational or illogical in using propensity reasoning to infer that an accused committed the act alleged.
Viewed in this way, the evidence of the accused's discreditable conduct is a form of circumstantial evidence and meets the legal relevance criterion [notes omitted].
33 This same rationale was articulated with respect to a product liability case by Wachowich A.C.J.
(as he then was) in KN v.
Alberta, 1999 ABQB 270 at para.

23, 243 AR 94: With manufactured products, if something is wrong with a machine causing it to produce defective widgets, transmissions or Cessnas, if the plaintiff's same widget, transmission or Cessna is defective in the same way, then other instances of similarly defective products produced by the same machine are highly relevant and probative, as there is a substantial likelihood that the defect in the product was produced by the defective machine.
Human behaviour is, fortunately, not so predictable or immutable.
34 In Trans-Border Plastics Ltd v.
Leavens Air Charter Ltd (1982), 36 OR (2d) 731 at 735, [1982] O.J.
No.

2565 (ON HCJ) [“Trans-Border Plastics”], the purchaser of a faulty Cessna airplane applied for an order requiring the defendant to produce “airplane condition reports possessed by Cessna in relation to all 421C aircraft and relating to conditions complained of in the action.” This included any reports on any 421C aircraft made at any time, which the defendant claimed was unnecessarily onerous and, therefore, subject to exclusion under the similar fact rule.
The Court stated at p.

735-36: … if defects of the nature complained of by the plaintiff are prevalent in other aircraft of the same model and manufactured pursuant to the same plans such evidence is relevant in the determination of the issue of whether the 421C aircraft has inherent defects.
Whether such evidence is admissible at the trial will be determined by the trial judge.

I am, however, persuaded by the decisions of the Alberta and British Columbia Courts that information concerning defects in other machines or in the component parts is relevant and such information should be disclosed at the discovery stage.
35 The Alberta decision referred to was Tachit v.
Versatile Mfg Ltd (1978), 11 AR 544 [“Tachit”].
In this case, the plaintiff claimed negligence in the manufacture of a tractor and sought any information regarding transmission problems in other similar tractors.
McFadyen J. found this was relevant, and cited MacDonald J. in Busslinger v.
Bow Valley Machinery (Calgary) Ltd, [1975] A.J.
No.

57, (6 February 1975) Calgary 101405 (AB Sup Ct) [“Busslinger”], as follows: … it is relevant in this case, when the defectiveness of a machine and whether or not there was negligence in its manufacture, assembly, distribution or sale is in issue, that the plaintiff seek the defendants' information as to the quality of the machine in question gained as a result of the tests that may have been conducted or similar things manufactured, assembled or distributed or sold by the defendants, and of the results of inspection of similar things, whether or not in any particular case such information is gained subsequent to the event in issue or not.
36 The Trans-Border Plastics, Tachit, and Busslinger cases are all “product liability” cases.
Although the cases predate the current wording of Rule 5.2, all dealt with the question of what is relevant at discovery, and all found the information at issue to be relevant and producible.

I find the information in these cases falls within today's definition of secondary relevance because the information ordered produced, was information from which the existence of primary facts could be directly inferred.
37 The Defendants have characterized the information being sought in this application as a search for tertiary or “similar fact evidence.” As such, they argue, it is inadmissible.
38 I agree with the Defendants that similar fact evidence is presumptively inadmissible.
See R. v.
That however does not make the information sought not relevant.
See for example R. v.
Batte, supra.
A number of other evidentiary principles must also be remembered.
First, evidence that is presumptively inadmissible for one purpose may be admissible for another purpose; see for example Cheyne v.
Alberta, 2003 ABQB 244.
Second, the admissibility of evidence is dependant on the context of the other trial evidence.
Therefore to my mind, the determination of admissibility of evidence is a function of the trial judge.
It is not the function of the case management judge: see TW v.
University of Alberta Hospital, 2000 ABQB 387 at para 28, 267 AR 169.
39 One of the issues at trial will be whether the Subject Pipe was negligently manufactured; that makes this a “product liability” case.

Thus, if defects of the nature complained of by CNRL are prevalent in other A106 Grade B pipe manufactured by Mittal at its Roman Mill, such evidence may well be relevant in determining whether the Subject Pipe was negligently manufactured.
40 From the evidence before me it is clear that Vass notified Mittal of five other quality incidents.
Other emails refer to “quality concerns”, materials shipped prior to July, 2005 as “unsure”, and corrective measures being implemented.
Mr.
Goel testified Mittal had retained Bureau Veritas on June 29, 2005 for its third party inspection of material for North America.
Those inspections began August 2005.

41 If there were manufacturing issues and/or inherent defects respecting the A106 Grade B pipe manufactured by Mittal at the Roman Mill during the same time-frame as that when the Subject Pipe was being made, this is evidence which could give rise to a very strong inference regarding the manner of the pipe's manufacture which could significantly help determine the negligence and breach of contract issues raised in CNRL's Statements of Claim, and as such it would qualify as “secondary” evidence as described by the Court of Appeal in NAC Constructors.
Therefore, I find the information sought by CNRL is relevant.
In Kaddoura v.
Hanson, 2015 ABCA 154, the Court dealt with two consolidated appeals which involved alleged mortgage fraud schemes.
The alleged scheme was alleged to work as follows: a fraudulent person (“the fraudster”) would agree to purchase a piece of land from the original owner at a fair market price.
The fraudster would then recruit a “straw buyer” who would agreed to purchase the land from the fraudster at an inflated value.
The property would then be transferred directly from the original owner to the straw buyer.
A financial institution would be induced to lend money and take a mortgage the amount of which would be based on the inflated value.
The money in excess of the original sale price would then be pocketed by the fraudster after the straw buyer is paid a fee for participating.
In the consolidated appeals before the Court of Appeal, the Royal Bank had been granted mortgages by persons alleged to be straw buyers.

When the mortgages went into default, the Bank commenced actions for the shortfalls against the alleged straw buyers (in whose names the properties were registered and who had granted the mortgages to the Bank), and the straw buyers then sued (or third partied) the lawyer who had represented the parties in the transactions.

The matter before the Court of Appeal related to the lawyer's appeal of a Master's order which required the lawyer to disclose the existence of certain documents on other files in which the lawyer had acted for the alleged fraudster.

The Court said: 11 The respondents' proposed line of argument is that if the lawyer was involved in numerous other files involving the same main fraudster, it would support an inference that the lawyer actually knew, or “ought to have known” that something illegitimate was going on.
In other words, the straw buyers seek to use circumstantial evidence to prove the state of mind or state of knowledge of the lawyers.
Irregularities in any one real estate file may simply be an aberration; a pattern of files with similar irregularities arguably calls for an explanation.
In order to support this line of argument, the straw buyers seek production of other client files in the lawyer's offices involving the same alleged main fraudster or bank loans officer.
The argument is that if those files disclose a pattern of irregularities, it will assist the straw buyers in proving one of the issues in the litigation.
12 The plaintiffs essentially seek “similar fact evidence” in the discovery process.
While that sort of evidence is more common in criminal cases, it can be used in civil cases as well.
Mood Music Publishing Co. v De Wolfe Ltd., [1976] Ch 119, [1976] 1 All ER 763 (CA), concerned allegations of breach of copyright.
The defendant pleaded that any similarity between its published work and that of the plaintiff was mere coincidence.
The plaintiff was permitted to use evidence of other breaches of copyright by the defendant in order to show a pattern of conduct.
The evidence was circumstantial evidence of the defendant's knowledge and intent.
13 This type of evidence was also used in Greenglass v Rusonik, [1983] OJ No 40 (CA), an action against solicitors over a complex real estate transaction.
An inflated sale price was one feature of the scheme.
Evidence that the defendant solicitors had participated in other similar transactions was admitted “to show system, state of mind, knowledge and intent” (at para.
If that sort of evidence can potentially be probative at trial, there is no reason in principle why it cannot be explored during the discovery process.

14 At the production stage of the litigation, it is not necessary to decide whether the trial judge will or will not be prepared to draw the inferences from the circumstantial evidence put forward by the respondents.
Nor must the respondents demonstrate conclusively that the discovered records will in fact contain any evidence of assistance to them.
It may be that the client files will be produced, be examined, and be shown to have no probative value under any theory of the case.
However, at this stage of the litigation the respondents need only show a plausible line of argument: Dow Chemical Canada ULC v Nova Chemicals Corp., 2014 ABCA 244 at para.
21, 577 AR 335; Weatherill (Estate) v Weatherill, 2003 ABQB 69 at para.
