paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.7:1 Rule 5.7 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.7. 1. Describing Records In Dorchak v. Krupka, 1997 ABCA 89, (sub nom. Roy v. Krilow) 196 A.R. 81 at pp. 84-94 [A.R.], Justice Côté discussed how to describe documents in an affidavit of records: The main issue here is how much detail an affidavit of documents must give about the individual documents which it discloses. . . . . . In both affidavits of documents, the producible and the privileged documents are described the same way. In each case, the description is very brief. I will quote one: “Documents mechanically numbered 000001 to 000020.”… Each appellant swore an affidavit and submits that the numbering is sufficient description. But each respondent (who sought the affidavit) seeks a detailed description of each individual document. Each respondent apparently seeks a list giving the nature, date, name of author, and name of recipient, of each document. . . . . . The cases seem to differ little respecting what are the basic principles The relevant Rules of Court are terse, and do not expressly call for much… These Rules establish discovery of documents, a valuable mechanism invented in Chancery centuries ago. It is intended to prevent destruction or suppression of evidence, get admissions for trial, prevent surprise, and prevent fabrication of written or oral evidence. An affidavit of documents must show unambiguously what documents' existence it does or does not disclose. It must remove any uncertainty on the following vital question. If a piece of paper turns up later, or is tendered on a motion or at trial, has it been disclosed by the previous affidavit of documents? That question can arise in a motion for a further and better affidavit of documents, under rule 194(1). It also arises when there is an objection to putting a document into evidence at trial, for failure to disclose it, under rule 195. It is important that the affidavit remove any doubt on the topic … Either of the methods suggested by the opposing parties here would fill that bill. If a document is in a bundle of individually numbered sheets, then it is easy to see from any the document's face and location that it is one of the documents disclosed [sic]. (If it is contended that it is an identical copy to a document produced, the one in the numbered bundle can be compared with it.) The numbering should be indelible, of course; pencilled numbers or flimsy tabs would not do: see Solid Waste v. Philips, supra, at 487. As our court said recently, such questions relate more to preservation than to discovery, and individual methods can be adapted in individual cases with different circumstances: Banque Nationale v. Cdn. Eng. & Surveys, supra. The respondents' rival plan to describe each document separately without marking it is not quite so unambiguous; for example, there could be two different memos to file bearing the same date. But it is probably good enough in most circumstances. Besides that rule of unambiguous identification, does any other principle of justice or rule of law apply? Where producible documents are concerned, I do not know of any. It seems to me that everything else is just a matter of mechanics, convenience, and common sense. . . . . . It is true that modern litigation management often benefits if each side in a complex suit prepares fairly detailed indexes of the truly important documents in the suit. Sometimes a chronology of documents will reveal many interesting things, and give a good framework for oral discoveries. But I see nothing in the Rules of Court or the decided cases saying that either lawyer must prepare such a tool for the other side. Still less need a lawyer do so for all the marginally relevant documents which an affidavit of documents must disclose. That is not the function of an affidavit of documents. Indeed, such a finding tool prepared by one side would plainly be privileged. If the two sides wish to eliminate duplication of effort by preparing such chronologies of important papers jointly, or by exchanging them, that is commendable. But the present Rules and decided cases do nothing to compel such cooperation or exchange. Banque Nationale de Paris (Can.) v. Cdn. Eng. & Surveys (Yukon), supra, involved millions of producible documents. In that case, a list of hundreds of numbered bundles, with no other indication of their contents, would not have sufficed. That would be even more true if the contents of the bundles were random, e.g. a company's files had been shuffled. But in the Banque Nationale case, there was no problem, because a card index and other finding tools had been provided. The courts held that sufficed. I doubt that the index listed every single document, but where documents are grouped in some meaningful way, that is surely not necessary. In a medium-sized suit, one often sees dozens of numbered bundles listed in the producible part of the affidavit of documents. If the affidavit gives no indication whatever of their contents, and no other finding tool is provided, that is very likely not a good enough description. It is not insufficient because it violates any particular rule of law, but simply because it is unworkable. However, an affidavit listing such numbered bundles would suffice if its producible schedule briefly explained the basic nature or source of each bundle. For example, it might say that one bundle contained the invoices and statements from the plaintiff to the defendant respecting the transactions and debts sued for. And it might say that another bundle contained the plaintiff's Lethbridge branch's correspondence file for 1997 respecting the defendant. And so forth. The odd stray document which was important but did not fit logically into any bundle might need separate description. What is an appropriate description or arrangement for a handful of producible documents may well not be appropriate for a roomful, and vice versa: Cdn. Eng. & Surveys (Yuk.) v. Banque Nationale de Paris (1995), 179 A.R. 394, ¶ 20, 22, 25; affd. (C.A.), supra. What is a suitable mode of description or identification depends a good deal upon the circumstances of the individual case: G.W.L. Properties Ltd. et al. v. Grace (W.R.) & Co.-Conn. (1992), 14 C.P.C. (3d) 74 (B.C. S.C.); leave denied (1993), 22 B.C.A.C. 78 (C.A.) … Our court has already rejected any rule which requires that individual documents always be individually listed: Banque Nationale v. Cdn. Eng., supra. . . . . . The orthodox law is all digested by Chitty in a detailed article in, [1924] 2 D.L.R. 1. The cases reported to then uniformly permit numbered bundles without lists of individual documents. Many of the later cases cite or quote Chitty's review with approval. Many cases on this topic cite Visa Internaltional Service Association v. Block Brothers Realty Ltd., [1983] 4 W.W.R. 665 (B.C. S.C.); affd. (1983), 64 B.C.L.R. (2d) 390 (C.A.). That case expressly permits producible documents to be discovered in bundles of similar sorts of papers, without individually listing the papers. (The Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal, which had nothing to do with producible documents: (1983), 64 B.C.L.R. (2d) 390.) In modern complex litigation with large numbers of producible documents, it is certainly permissible to group them into bundles or groups with common characteristics, and to describe the groups without itemizing individual documents: G.W.L. Props. v. W.R. Grace, supra. For all these reasons, I cannot agree that the appellants need have listed and described the producible documents individually, if it was convenient to number them mechanically and treat them as a group. . . . . . Such a long list is totally unworkable… But if instead the affidavit lists correspondence files by subject or time period or office, and lists bundles of other documents such as invoices or reports by type and age, then almost any document can readily be located. Even thousands of producible documents can be sensibly described and readily found in a two-page list of a few dozen numbered bundles of similar papers arranged by topic. Such a list takes under a minute to read. For that reason, the English courts have consistently held that a large number of producible documents must be arranged by characteristics and described by numbered bundles. They must not be individually described in a bulky inventory; such a fat list of individual documents is an abuse of process: Walker v. Poole (1882), 21 Ch. D. 835; Hill v. Hart-Davis (1884), 26 Ch. D. 470 (C.A.). If long individual lists were too awkward and slow in that more leisurely gaslit age, they are an abomination in today's more congested courts. In accord is G.W.L. v. W.A. Grace, supra. This court recently refused to order such individual listing of producible documents, in a large suit, in Banque Nationale v. Cdn. Eng. & Surveys, supra. It doubted that there was even a presumption in favour of listing documents individually. . . . . . Now I will turn to the privileged documents. Here also, the first principle is seeing whether one can unequivocally say of a given piece of paper whether its existence has been disclosed in the affidavit or not. And many of the questions of convenience are broadly similar. Here again, a numbered bundle fills the bill at least as well as individual descriptions. But privilege imports a second principle of law. Privilege is an important substantive rule of law, not to be frittered away: Descoteaux et al. v. Mierzwinski et al., [1982] 1 S.C.R. 860 … Therefore, it is beside the point to speak of the modern tendency to widen discovery, or to imply that privilege is old-fashioned: those fallacies are demolished in Hodgkinson v. Sims (1988), 33 B.C.L.R. (2d) 129, 134–36 (C.A.) … Any system of listing or describing privileged documents which gives away privileged information is therefore unthinkable. There is considerable danger of giving away secrets by describing the individual privileged documents: see London & Midland General Insurance Co. v. Lambert, [1972] 1 W.W.R. 224 (Alta. Dist. Ct.) 226, and cases there cited… . . . . . Furthermore, in this age of photocopying and e-mail, people rarely write out long recitals. They write short letters or memos, and attach relevant existing documents. To force a person to list what documents were attached to a privileged document would often be to reveal virtually all the contents of the privileged communication. To describe a document as a blueprint, an X- ray, a tracing or log from certain scientific apparatus, or as a videotape or a tape recording, often will give away the whole secret. The danger of giving away privileged secrets means that the description of the privileged documents need not include dates, contents, or parties to them: Curlett v. Canadian Fire Insurance Co. (No. 2), [1938] 3 W.W.R. 429, 431-2 (Alta. T.D.). Cf. London & Midland v. Lambert, supra. I reiterate that such individual details are not necessary to prove whether the existence of a given privileged document is revealed by the affidavit of documents. A bundle of numbered papers suffices. Indeed, because consecutive document numbers are unambiguous, they are slightly better for that purpose than word descriptions of individual documents: see Solid Waste v. Philip, supra. One must not apply uncritically to privileged documents reported cases involving only producible documents, such as G.W.L. v. W.A. Grace, supra, or Cdn. Eng. & Surveys v. Banque Nationale de Paris, supra. As noted, cases on producible documents depend largely on convenience, not law. And revealing information about producible documents is good, subject to expense and convenience. But revealing information about privileged documents is dangerous. Occasionally one will find a decided case suggesting briefly that the description of individual privileged documents in an affidavit of documents must be full enough to let the court or the opponent assess whether privilege is properly claimed in respect of each document… In my view, that suggestion of law is wrong. The description of the documents in the schedule need not corroborate privilege… . . . . . I would not follow Creaser v. Warren (1987), 77 N.S.R. (2d) 429 (C.A.). It required that the affidavit set out the status of the sender and recipient of each document said to be privileged…Creaser is distinguishable. It simply applies a Nova Scotia Rule of Court which expressly calls for a “description of each document”. Alberta's Rules contain no such requirement… . . . . . So ordinarily it is sufficient for the affidavit's second part of the first schedule to list and describe privileged documents merely as numbered bundles. Details of individual documents are unnecessary… . . . . . I do not wish to leave the impression that it would suffice merely to describe the privileged papers in a big suit as “5287 sheets numbered in red 1 to 5287”. One would expect some kind of identification of the bundles in a bigger suit… It is a question of practicality. For example, papers generated by counsel for the purpose of this suit after it existed or was contemplated are plainly privileged. There is no reason not to say one bundle is counsel's file. Indeed saying so might avoid a lot of suspicion, requests that the court examine the documents under rule 194, and so forth. Ordinarily one should be able to describe a file or bundle in some manner which will not reveal secrets. For example … one may call it a lawyer's file without naming the lawyer. . . . . . Quite aside from a list of mechanically numbered papers, the list of privileged documents in the Schedule of each affidavit contains a second item in these words: Documents, correspondence, memoranda, briefs, communications, proofs, working-papers, photographs, plans, diagrams and miscellaneous documents forming Counsel's brief. … This is a mere vague reference to correspondence with solicitors or to documents for litigation… It is completely insufficient, if there are no numbered bundles or other description. How could one ever later tell whether a given paper was one of the documents which had been referred to so vague and generic a way? … Up to this point, the topic has been how to describe the documents now (or formerly) in the party's possession or power. A completely different topic is what reasons for any claim of privilege in the body of the affidavit of documents. Rule 188(b) says: The affidavit … shall state … the party objects to produce and the grounds for any such objection, … The reasons must be fairly precise, and must recite enough facts to trigger privilege. For example, if the body of the affidavit refers to three kinds of privilege (solicitor's advice, litigation, and without-prejudice), it should indicate which papers fall within which. Nor is it enough to speak of communications with a solicitor; one must swear that they were for the purpose of getting advice. Nor is it enough to say that papers were for the purpose of resisting a claim; one must also say they were created when the claim existed or was contemplated. Here each affidavit refers to at least two different types of privilege, and does not say which paper falls within which category: I object to produce the said documents on the following grounds: (a) Material obtained for or by Counsel in contemplation of litigation; and (b) Privileged professional communications of a confidential character passing between Counsel, third parties and Client for the purpose of giving and taking legal advice and arising in contemplation of litigation. That will not do. The individual types of privilege must be segregated, and the affidavit must say which numbered documents come within each type of privilege. Madam Justice Veit, in Canadian Engineering & Surveys (Yukon) Ltd. v. Banque Nationale de Paris (Canada) (1995), 179 A.R. 394 (Q.B.), said at p. 395: Where a large number of documents is subject to discovery, those documents need not be individually listed and described. Her Ladyship then listed the principles to be applied when disclosing records. At p. 398, she said: In summary, therefore, the case law establishes the following principles: Disclosure of documents must: • be assessed from the perspective of the party requiring production rather than from the perspective of the party providing the documents; • be meaningful, reliable, and complete; • provide sufficient detail to enable the party requiring disclosure to understand generally what the documents contain, where they originated, when they originated, and the number of documents within the group; • allow the party requiring disclosure to retrieve the documents; • allow the party requiring disclosure to object to the tendering of any document into evidence at trial on the grounds that it had not been produced; • be appropriate to the circumstances of the particular case; • be more descriptive than mere numbering. An appeal of Madam Justice Veit's decision was dismissed [see: (1996), 196 A.R. 1 (C.A.)]. At p. 2, Kerans J.A. said: Mr. Lebo sought an order from the case manager that the engineering firm be required to list and number every document and provide a brief description. The case manager refused this request and accepted the argument that the filing system of the engineering firm, properly understood, was adequate to direct a person to whichever documents that they may wish to examine. Mr. Lebo has not persuaded us that we ought to interfere with the order made. We agree with the statement of principles summarized by the chambers judge at pages six and seven of her decision, and we agree that the production of documents involves sufficient detail to enable the party requiring disclosure to understand generally what the documents contain, when they originated, where they originated, and the number of documents within the group, among other requirements. We do not accept Mr. Lebo's argument that this means that the order sought by him should be made here. Although Mr. Lebo states that past cases declare that the generation of a numbered list of descriptive [sic] is the general rule from which one only makes exceptions, we are not so sure this can be said any longer in cases involving millions of documents. The chambers judge has, of course, not exhausted her jurisdiction. If Mr Lebo is able to persuade her that he has a specific problem finding a specific category of documents, she yet can grant relief. An inquiry of that sort involves, in part, not only the notice to produce but the examinations for discovery. We accept that when a party relies on its own filing system as a means to display documents in a meaningful manner, then it falls to that party to make reasonable efforts to explain and clarify that filing system to a stranger. Generally speaking, filing systems are not as understandable to strangers than they are to insiders. Another point made by Mr. Lebo is that for purposes of integrity and security, all documents should be marked with an identifying mark and a note made of the sequence of documents within the files. This is a practice that would be mutually beneficial in most litigation cases, but it is an issue that is separate from the question of production and examination. It relates more to preservation. 2. Bundling Documents In Starratt v. Chandran, 2023 ABKB 609, Justice Feasby discussed “bundling” of records under Rule 5.7 (which was brought into effect after Dorchak v. Krupka, 1997 ABCA 89, (sub nom. Roy v. Krilow) 196 A.R. 81 at pp. 84-94 [A.R.], was decided): [18] Justice Côté explained in Dorchak v Krupka, 1997 ABCA 89 at para 8 that an “affidavit of documents must show unambiguously what documents' existence it does or does not disclose.” He referred to this in para 12 as the “rule of unambiguous identification.” He concluded that unambiguous identification could be accomplished by either numbering or describing each record. [19] Justice Côté went on to observe at para 16 that where “documents are grouped in some meaningful way” an index listing every single document is not necessary. He held at para 18 that “an affidavit listing such numbered bundles would suffice if its producible schedule briefly explained the basic nature or source of each bundle.” Dorchak appears to permit bundling records of the same nature or from the same source. [20] Following Dorchak, a new version of the Rules was adopted. Rule 5.7 modifies the law discussed in Dorchak. … [21] The practice of bundling records is justified in Dorchak partly on the basis that sometimes, in cases with a large volume of records, it is too laborious to describe each individual record. This reality has been overtaken in most large-scale litigation by what is referred to as e-Discovery, in which document production is often outsourced to specialized service providers who make extensive use of technology including Artificial Intelligence (AI). In cases where record numbering and descriptions are generated by a computer, saving labour does not provide much justification for bundling. [22] Today, bundling is most often seen in cases like the present one, where a party is required to produce hard copy records and is financially strapped. Ms. Hami, a legal assistant working for counsel for the Defendants, deposed that record production was hampered by the Defendants' lack of funds. Bundling, though often sub-optimal for the efficient resolution of disputes, is a justifiable expedient for under-resourced litigants. With that said, Courts must be alive to the potential abuse of the practice of bundling by recalcitrant litigants who use bundling as a strategy to conceal records and obstruct their adversaries. …. [26] The adequacy of the descriptions provided is inextricably intertwined with the next question, which is whether the bundled records are “all of the same nature” as required by Rule 5.7(2)(a). There is no judicial consideration of the meaning of the term “of the same nature” in Alberta or in the other provinces and Federal Court where the same prerequisite to bundling exists. [27] The “same nature” requirement was adopted as a corrective to Dorchak which was viewed by the civil litigation bar as allowing over-bundling that “leads to cross-examinations on affidavits and prolongs examinations for discovery”: Alberta Law Reform Institute, Alberta Rules of Court Project: Document Discovery and Examination for Discovery, Consultation Memorandum No. 12.2 (October 2002) at 27. The ALRI report at page 29 recommended the adoption of the “same nature” concept from the Federal Court Rules though without any explanation of what the idea meant. All that can be taken from the ALRI report is that “same nature” was intended to be more restrictive than the “meaningful grouping” concept in Dorchak. [28] A textual reading of Rule 5.7(2) also suggests that “same nature” is a narrower concept than “meaningful grouping.” Records of a different nature – for example, an agreement and a photograph – may be gathered in a meaningful grouping if there is some other logic that connects the records. The Plaintiffs argued that records of the same nature means that they are the same type or class of record and should be from a defined period. For example, an appropriate bundle would be “Statements for CIBC Account 1234-56789 for 2022.” Another example of an appropriate bundle would be “Invoices Issued by XYZ Corp in January 2023.” Even in some situations it may be appropriate to bundle hard copy correspondence as, for example, “Correspondence Received by A.B.C. from September 1, 2021 to December 31, 2021.” Such bundles can be succinctly described, are an efficient way to produce records for the producing party, and do not compromise the receiving party's ability to understand what is being produced. Such an approach is efficient and consistent with the purpose and intention of the Rules as stated in Rule 1.2. [29] The Plaintiffs submit that Rule 5.7 should be interpreted consistent with its text and with a pragmatic and functional understanding of the record production process. Records of the “same nature” (i.e. homogeneous) can efficiently be “described in sufficient detail to enable another party to understand what it contains” whereas a bundle of disparate records (i.e. heterogeneous) requires a comprehensive description of the contents of the bundle to achieve the same effect. …. [31] Given the longstanding practice in Alberta, reflected in Dorchak and Blough [Blough v. Busy Music Inc. 2018 ABQB 560], of bundling records received from a common source, I cannot read “same nature” as to restrict the practice of bundling only to situations where there is the same type or class of record such as bank statements or invoices. Records from a common source may be of the same nature, particularly where, as in the present case, there are other characteristics identified that connect the bundled records. Such an interpretation also maintains the flexibility that bundling provides for parties that are financially constrained. [32] Though the disputed records may be bundled, that does not end the analysis. Rule 5.7(2)(b) imposes a duty on the disclosing party to describe the bundle “in sufficient detail to enable another party to understand what it contains.” The approach to describing bundles must be adjusted depending on the context; the principle of proportionality that governs record production applies to the description of bundles. Where a bundle is comprised of homogeneous records (e.g. bank statements from a single account for a defined period) a terse description is all that is needed. The more heterogeneous the contents of a bundle, the more robust the description required. This is an example of what Justice Marion, writing about a different aspect of record production, called “common sense and proportionality”: MBH v CKI, 2023 ABKB 284 at para 40. 3. Identification of Privileged Documents In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. ShawCor Ltd., 2014 ABCA 289, 2014 CarswellAlta 1582, 580 A.R. 265, 2 Alta. L.R. (6th) 146, 376 D.L.R. (4th) 581, the Court of Appeal gave direction on how to describe in an affidavit of records those documents over which privilege is claimed. At paragraphs 8-9, 36, 41, 50-51, 72-73, and 92, the Court said: 8 We have concluded that a party preparing an affidavit of records must, short of revealing information that is privileged, provide a sufficient description of each record for which privilege is claimed to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege. While the objective is to reduce the need for parties to seek recourse to other time-consuming and costly litigation steps, we are equally satisfied that this can be accomplished in a manner that does not injure valid privileges. In addition, where a judge is nevertheless called on to determine privilege issues, a sufficient description of records will assist the judge in determining whether a more probing assessment is required and, if so, the confines of that assessment. 9 This result is premised on a number of specific conclusions. Rule 5.7 was intended to apply to all relevant and material records, even those a party objects to produce. Thus, in an affidavit of records, a party must number all records in a convenient manner and briefly describe them (Rule 5.7(1)). The right to bundle and treat that bundle as a single record under Rule 5.7(2) applies equally to records over which privilege is claimed. Rule 5.8 imposes additional responsibilities on a party who objects to produce a prima facie producible record. The particular ground(s) of the objection must be identified with respect to each record in order to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege. That means the party must state the actual privilege being relied upon with respect to that record and describe the record in a way that, without revealing information that is privileged, indicates how the record fits within the claimed privilege. These requirements apply equally to a bundled record over which a party claims privilege. … 36 Rules 5.6, 5.7 and 5.8 lie at the heart of this dispute. As noted above, we have concluded that a grammatical, purposive and contextual reading of these Rules imposes on a party the obligation to number and briefly describe each record that is relevant and material, including those it claims are privileged. In accordance with Schedule 2 of Form 26, those latter records should be set out in separate categories as contemplated therein. A party is entitled to bundle privileged records providing that the bundled record otherwise meets the requirements of Rule 5.7. For records that a party claims are privileged, the party must, in accordance with Rule 5.8, identify the particular grounds of the objection to production for each record in order to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege. That means the party must state the actual privilege being relied upon with respect to that record and describe the record in a way that, without revealing information that is privileged, indicates how the record fits within the claimed privilege. These requirements apply equally to a bundled record over which a party claims privilege. … … [41] It follows that we do not view Rules 5.7 and 5.8 as creating discrete obligations and rights depending on whether a party objects to produce records. Rather, despite any ambiguity suggested by their headings, we are satisfied that Rule 5.7 was intended to apply to all relevant and material records that are prima facie producible and that Rule 5.8 was intended to impose additional, not separate, obligations on a party who objects to producing a prima facie producible record. What further information does Rule 5.8 require a party to disclose for records over which privilege is claimed? The answer is that it requires, in particular, that a party identify the “grounds for the objection in respect of each record”. … [50] As noted, we have concluded that each record over which privilege is claimed must be (i) numbered in a convenient order and (ii) described in a way that, without revealing privileged information, indicates how that record fits within the claimed privilege. However, this requirement to describe each record individually is subject to the proviso that relevant and material records of the same nature can be bundled and treated as a single record so long as the requirements of Rule 5.7(2) are met. That is, the description offered for the bundle must be sufficiently clear so as to allow another party to understand what it contains. In addition, given the requirements of Rule 5.8, this description must also provide sufficient facts to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege over the bundle in question. [51] Bundling can be effective even with multiple claims of privilege. To illustrate, consider a party who claims privilege over 50 records. After describing the bundle in sufficient detail to enable another party to understand what it contains and providing sufficient information to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege over the bundle in question, the party objecting to disclosure identifies records 1 to 30 as subject to solicitor-client privilege, records 40 to 50 as litigation privilege and records 31 to 39 as both. This permits a party to identify which form(s) of privilege attaches to each record while recognizing that some records might have multiple reasons for objection, any one of which may be sufficient: see Opron Construction Co. v Alberta (1989), 1989 ABCA 279 (CanLII), 100 AR 58 (CA) at para 5. Another party would be assisted by this degree of specificity and might well choose to accept the objections, or only resist them selectively. A judge reviewing the records under Rule 5.11 would also be in a better position to organize the evaluation of the objections. … [72] In summary, records where privilege is asserted must now be dealt with individually. Each record must be numbered in a convenient order and briefly described, short of disclosing privileged information. Records may be bundled where privilege is being asserted providing that the bundled record otherwise meets the requirements of Rule 5.7. In accordance with Rule 5.8, a party must also identify the grounds for claiming privilege with respect to each record in order to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claim. This latter requirement means that, for each record, a party must state the particular privilege being asserted and describe the record in a way, again without revealing information that is privileged, that indicates how the record fits within the claimed privilege. The description of all relevant and material records over which privilege is claimed should be set out in Schedule 2 of Form 26 in the separate categories contemplated therein. [73] CNRL's affidavits do not comply with these requirements. Harvey's first affidavit made a blanket claim of privilege over an undisclosed number of documents and merely listed the privilege categories set out in Schedule 2 of Form 26, with nothing added except the word “NIL” in reference to the “Other” category. While Harvey's later affidavit disclosed the number of records over which privilege was claimed, namely 1,058, and stated that these records fell into five discrete categories, this too falls well short of what is required under the Rules. It follows that the appeal must be allowed. CNRL is directed to prepare a new or supplementary affidavit in compliance with the Rules and this judgment. … [92] Without limiting what we have said, we summarize for convenience the requirements of the Rules discussed above relating to affidavits of records and privilege claims. We stress that this is not intended to be an exhaustive list of those requirements: 1. Every relevant and material record is prima facie producible and the minimum requirements and rights under Rule 5.7(1) and (2) apply to all such records, even where a party objects to production based on claimed privilege or some other legal ground. 2. Every relevant and material record must be numbered in a convenient order and briefly described. These should be set out in the separate Schedules applicable to each as contemplated in Form 26. Accordingly, a party claiming privilege over a number of records must number and briefly describe each record short of revealing information that is privileged. The description of those records should be set out in Schedule 2 of Form 26 in the separate categories contemplated therein. 3. A party is permitted to bundle and treat as a single record a group of records that are all of the same nature so long as the bundle is, in accordance with Rule 5.7(2)(b), described in sufficient detail to enable another party to understand what it contains. This bundling option also applies to records over which a party claims privilege. 4. If a party objects to the disclosure of otherwise relevant and material records, it shall, in addition to numbering the records in a convenient order and briefly describing them, set forth the grounds for objection in respect of each record to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege. In doing so, the party is required to (i) state the actual privilege being relied upon with respect to that record; and (ii) describe the record in a way that, without revealing privileged information, indicates how the record fits within the claimed privilege. These requirements also apply to a bundled record over which a party claims privilege. In Alberta v. Suncor Energy Inc., 2017 ABCA 221, 2017 CarswellAlta 1173, 54 Alta. L.R. (6th) 237, within hours of a worker dying at a Suncor worksite, the company launched an internal investigation into the events. In a subsequent government Occupational Health and Safety investigation, Suncor claimed both solicitor-client privilege and litigation privilege over documents it refused to produce. The Court of Appeal's comments about how to describe documents for which such privilege claims are also applicable to Rule 5.7. The Court said, at paragraphs 45–49: 45 Suncor asserted both solicitor-client and litigation privilege over nearly all of the documents it refused to produce. Although documents may frequently be subject to both forms of privilege, Suncor must independently distinguish whether solicitor-client or litigation privilege applies, in order to permit a meaningful assessment and review of each bundle of documents. Making a blanket assertion that both forms of privilege apply, in instances where one or the other is clearly unavailable, is a litigation tactic that ought to be discouraged. 46 Parties must describe the documents in a way that indicates the basis for their claim: ShawCor at para 9. The grounds for claiming solicitor-client privilege and litigation privilege are distinct. A description that supports one class of privilege does not necessarily support the other. 47 To support a claim of solicitor-client privilege, Suncor must at least describe the documents in a manner that indicates communications between a client and a legal advisor related to seeking or receiving legal advice. 48 To support a claim of litigation privilege, Suncor must describe documents with enough particularity to indicate whether the dominant purpose for their creation was in contemplation of litigation. 49 In conclusion, we find that the chambers judge erred in finding that the documents were sufficiently described to allow an assessment of the privilege claims. The comments in ShawCor at para 63 apply equally to the OHS context: the claim of privilege is based on the honour system, and reasonable people can disagree as to whether particular material is privileged. The eight categories of material claimed as privileged by Suncor are not particularized to identify whether and how it claims the material was created in contemplation of litigation. As noted above, material created in the ordinary course of business and later collected for the investigation file, may arguably not be covered by litigation privilege. Of course, this does not require Suncor to describe the document in a way that undermines the privilege claimed. … 54 However, the chambers judge erred in finding that the documents were sufficiently described to allow an assessment of the privilege claims. Suncor must independently distinguish the nature of the legal privilege claimed, and the evidentiary basis for the claim, in order to allow for a meaningful assessment. The eight categories of material Suncor claims as privileged are not sufficiently particularized to identify whether the material was created in contemplation of litigation, as opposed to merely gathered or collected for that purpose. In Kaddoura v. Hanson, 2015 ABCA 154 (for a summary of the facts, see the annotation “Similar Fact Evidence” under Rule 5.6), the Court dealt with the submission that for a lawyer to even disclose the existence of a document held in his or her capacity as a lawyer for a client would violate the client's solicitor-client privilege: 19 The main basis of the lawyers' objection to the disclosure of the client records relates to issues of confidentiality and privilege. It is not disputed that solicitor and client privilege is one of the most carefully guarded principles of our legal system: Canada (Privacy Commissioner) v Blood Tribe Department of Health, 2008 SCC 44 at para. 9, [2008] 2 SCR 574; Canada (Attorney General) v Federation of Law Societies of Canada, 2015 SCC 7 at paras. 44, 120; University of Calgary v JR, 2015 ABCA 118 at para. 19. The contents of a solicitor's file will presumptively be privileged, subject to a very narrow list of exceptions. As a collateral argument, the lawyers argue that, for similar reasons, the client files are not under their “control”, an issue discussed below. The Law Society of Alberta has intervened on these issues. 20 The appellants and the Law Society argue that i) the Master's order compromises the privilege over the files; ii) the files are third party records and should only be obtained using the procedure under R 5.13; and iii) the Master's order was made without notice being given to the clients. 21 The Rules on the production of records recognize that privilege may be asserted over some records, and specifically deal with the issue. As noted, the Rules draw a distinction between the “disclosure” of records and the subsequent “production” of records. Under R. 5.6 a party must “disclose all records”, or in other words must make a list of them all. Rule 5.6(2)(b) recognizes that there may be valid objections to “producing” certain records, but still requires the litigants to “disclose” or list them. Rule 5.8 confirms that if a party objects to production of any records, they must still be identified in some suitable manner, and disclosed. Rule 5.11(1)(b) then states that the court can rule on any claim of privilege before the record is actually produced for inspection. 22 The concerns of the appellants and the Law Society are addressed by the structure of the Rules. The Master did not order the production of any records, only their disclosure or listing. The Master specifically declined (at para. 33) to consider any issue of privilege, recognizing that the review of the claim for privilege under R. 5.11(1)(b) would follow later. The formal order specifically states that issues of privilege are left for future consideration. 23 It can be argued that the mere listing of the client files involves some inroad into privilege: Thompson v Canada (Minister of National Revenue), 2013 FCA 197 at paras. 41-2, 366 DLR (4th) 169, argued and reserved SCC #35590. That may be so, but the Rules of Court nevertheless require that they be disclosed, even if not eventually produced because of a valid claim of privilege. Exceptions to solicitor and client privilege are not easily recognized, but when an enactment specifically calls for disclosure, the enactment prevails. The chambers judge modified the Master's order to the extent of allowing the files to be disclosed anonymously, a modification which effectively mitigated any objection that might be made on this ground. 24 Thus the appellants' arguments about breaches of privilege are premature. No court has yet ordered that the respondents are entitled to see these files. Likewise, the clients have not been effectively deprived of their claim to privilege or confidentiality, or notice of the application. When an application is brought for production of the files, it will probably be prudent to give the clients notice. Any dispute about the need for, method of, or extent of notice can be resolved at that time. Whether disclosure of the files is eventually adjudicated by an application under R. 5.11(1)(b) or R. 5.13 makes little difference if the clients are given notice either way. 25 There is a chicken-and-egg aspect to the appellants' position. The respondents do not want to see or review every file in the offices of the defendant lawyers. They are only interested in real estate files involving the same alleged main fraudster and bank loans officer. If the respondents were really required to proceed under R. 5.13 relating to the production of documents of third parties, and if they could only proceed on notice to the other straw buyer clients, how would they know which clients to serve with the application? If they are not entitled to a list of the relevant records, they would be forced to give notice to every client of the lawyers. Under the Master's order, there will be a discrete target list of clients who have files that are said to be within the scope of relevance. This is undoubtedly why the Rules require that even privileged documents be listed, with issues of production and privilege deferred until later. … 38 The Law Society also notes that its Code of Conduct places an obligation on a lawyer to protect the confidentiality of the client's files. Such provisions do not, however, automatically exempt a lawyer from any competing legal obligations to disclose information, for example under valid search warrants. General requirements of confidentiality do not necessarily excuse disclosure otherwise required by the Rules: 783783 Alberta Ltd. v Canada (Attorney General), 2010 ABCA 226 at para. 32, 29 Alta LR (5th) 37, 482 AR 136; D. v National Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Children, [1978] AC 171 at pp. 218–20 (HL). Rule 2.03(1)(b) of the Code of Conduct of the Law Society recognizes that by allowing disclosure when “required by law or a court”. Rule 2.03(4) of the Code of Conduct permits disclosure of confidential information in defence of allegations that the lawyer is civilly liable with respect to a matter involving a client's affairs, or may have committed acts of professional negligence. The issue is not whether lawyers have an obligation to keep their clients' files confidential, but whether the competing obligation to disclose documents under the Rules of Court prevails. The Rules provide a two-step process for resolving such issues. The first step requires that the lawyer list the relevant files in the Affidavit of Records, to create a platform for resolution of the ultimate issue. 4. Translating Documents Into English In Attila Dogan Construction & Installation Co. v. AMEC Americas Ltd., 2011 ABQB 794, 2011 CarswellAlta 2193, 530 A.R. 264, 64 Alta. L.R. (5th) 88, the Affidavit of Records produced by the Plaintiff contained a large number of documents written in the Turkish language. A dispute arose as to which party bore the responsibility of translating the documents into English. At paragraphs 61–63, Wittmann, C.J.Q.B. said: 61 AD contends that the law is clear that there is no obligation on the party producing documents to translate them into English, and that this is the sole responsibility of the party intending to lead the evidence at trial. AD relies upon Kellogg Co. v. Imperial Oil Ltd. (1996), 29 O.R. (3d) 70 (Gen. Div.), wherein Kitely J. held that correspondence and other written materials relevant to the issue of confusion between two trademarks in foreign countries should be produced, and further noted, at para.46, “There is no obligation on the party producing the documents to translate them into English; that will be the responsibility of the party who leads the evidence at trial.” Similarly, in Bilfinger Berger (Canada) Inc. v. Greater Vancouver Water District, 2010 BCSC 1104, [2010] B.C.J. No. 1586, Griffin J. held at paras.17 and 19: In my view, absent agreement between the parties, the Metro Vancouver [defendants] cannot transfer the burden of hiring their own interpreter if they wish to translate to English the documents produced to them. They can hopefully manage that cost by having an interpreter assist them with an informal translation without necessarily having a formal certified translation of each German language document. When, through the use of their interpreter, the Metro Vancouver parties determine which documents are most relevant to their case, they may wish to confirm their translation of those documents by agreement or through the examination for discovery process. … I further observe that these parties were in a sophisticated commercial relationship. These types of contracts often anticipate litigation and have agreements as to a court's jurisdiction or arbitration, for example. The Metro Vancouver parties knew that they were entering into a contractual relationship with a party that had many German employees. Metro Vancouver did have the opportunity to request a contractual term that if litigation between them did ensue Bilfinger Berger would be required to translate any of its German documents into English. Presumably solicitors in the future may wish to consider such a term. 62 AD has provided a number of authorities from the U.S. Federal Courts. While in Stapleton v. Kawasaki Heavy Industries Ltd. (1975), 69 F.R.D. 489 it was held that foreign companies should consider the cost of translating documents into English for the purpose of litigation as part of the “cost of transacting business” in the United States, that approach has fallen out of favour and instead the general rule is that, consistent with the principle that each party must bear the burden of financing their own suit, the cost of translating documents is to be borne by the party intending to use them: In re Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority (1982), 687 F. 2d 501; Cook v. Volkswagen of American Inc. (1984), 101 F.R.D. 92. 63 Ultimately, absent exceptional circumstances, any expenses incurred in the translating of documents in this action will be a taxable disbursement to be included in the Bill of Costs of the prevailing party. The issue is which of these parties should bear the cost in the interim. The authorities suggest that this should be the party seeking the documents, which is AMEC. But these authorities are neither binding nor particularly helpful. This action is at the disclosure stage. What is needed is a practical solution which furthers the management of the case. At paragraphs 66-67, his Lordship set out a practical solution: 66 On the issue of translation and the Turkish Documents, it occurs to me that Calgary counsel for AD are not fluent in the Turkish language. Therefore, perhaps the approximate 25,000 Turkish Documents, deemed relevant and material, by virtue of, and in accordance with, Rule 5.6(1)(b), must have already been translated and reviewed for compliance with this rule by Calgary counsel. So, if AD wishes to avoid putting up further security for costs for the disbursements incurred by AMEC for translation of the Turkish Documents in their entirety, copies of the translated Turkish Documents in English, if they exist, could be sent to AMEC and AMEC could then decide whether to accept the documents as translated. To the extent that the Turkish Documents, already translated into English, by agreement, might constitute a valid translation, the purpose articulated in Rule 1.2(1) quoted above is furthered. It would avoid the possibility of two different translations into English being presented, or worse still, disputed later, or at the trial. 67 There may however, be some documents which AMEC wishes to test in terms of the validity of the translation done by AD. If that process is engaged, AMEC would then bear the cost of testing the translation, subject to any further Order of the Court, depending on the result of the test. Chief Justice Wittmann's ruling was appealed to the Court of Appeal. The Court summarized the appellant's position at paragraph 6: 6 The appellant's argument can be summarized as follows: a party producing documents at the pre-trial stage in a language other than English is under no obligation to translate them and the case management judge erred by requiring the producing party, the appellant in this case, to post security for the translation costs. The Court of Appeal was not of the view that Chief Justice Wittmann had set out a general rule on the topic. At paragraph 8, the Court said: 8 The appellant argues that the case management judge erred in law in determining that there is an obligation on the party producing relevant and material foreign language documents to translate them. We do not believe the case management judge's order ought to be interpreted so broadly. He ruled that, on these facts, the initial cost of translation would be borne by the party wishing the documents to be translated, namely the respondent. But, given his prior security for costs decision and the anticipated significant cost of translating thousands of documents, he ordered that security be deposited for the actual costs incurred. At paragraphs 13–18, the Court of Appeal endorsed the Chief Justice's practical solution: 13 The appellant also argued that the case management judge failed to consider and apply rule 5.2(2) of the Rules, thereby erroneously deeming the Turkish documents relevant and material and that this contributed to his error in ordering security. 14 Rule 5.2(2) states that the disclosure or production of a document is not, by reason of that fact alone, to be considered an acknowledgment that the document is relevant or material. On the other hand, Rule 5.6(1) provides that an affidavit of records must disclose all relevant and material records. So, notwithstanding that disclosure of a document is not an acknowledgment of its relevance or materiality, the disclosing party still has the obligation to assess what records it considers may be or are relevant and material. 15 The case management judge was said to have assumed incorrectly that some of the documents had already been translated in order to enable appellant's counsel to assess their relevance and materiality. At the hearing of the appeal we were advised that none of the Turkish documents had been translated. 16 It would be our view that there would have had to have been a degree of translation in order for counsel for the producing party to have some understanding of what the records being produced were and some understanding of their relevance and materiality. Counsel have an obligation in that regard. A determination of prima facie relevance and materiality must be made. Indeed, Rule 5.2(1)(a) and (b) instructs counsel and their clients as to how to make that determination. And, ultimately, a formal affidavit must be sworn setting forth “relevant and material records”. 17 We do not believe that the case management judge was labouring under any misapprehension or that any misapprehension on his part contributed to his decision. In our view, all the case management judge was suggesting was that, as a practical solution, the appellant share any understanding it had acquired by virtue of having undergone the process of identifying relevant and material documents with a view to keeping the respondent's translation costs down. That was not unreasonable. 18 Further, until questioning takes place, the respondent will not know why the appellant produced the documents it produced. Some documents may have been produced because the appellant considered they might have relevance or materiality. Other documents may have been produced because the appellant knows now that it intends to rely on them at trial. The latter documents will clearly have to be translated. But in the meantime, the respondent needs to have some understanding of the import of all the documents produced and that will require some translation. The Court then made these additional suggestions (paragraphs 23–27): 23 While we are loathe to interfere with the case management judge's management of this case, we are concerned about the number of Turkish documents disclosed and the consequences of having either party bear the cost of translating them. So, we would suggest that the appellant be given the opportunity to produce a further and better affidavit of records after a further review of its documents. In oral argument, it was suggested that there may have been considerable duplication in the appellant's production. It is perhaps also the case that, out of an abundance of caution, more documents were produced than necessary. It may be that some of the 25,000 Turkish documents produced are not relevant or material and therefore do not require translation. Now knowing that it might have to bear the cost of translating some or all of the documents it disclosed, the appellant may wish an opportunity to revisit its affidavit of records. A culling of production could reduce the amount of translation required and correspondingly the quantum of security that need be posted. 24 If reducing the number of documents disclosed is not possible, the appellant might be given the opportunity to assist the respondent in understanding what documents it produced in its affidavit of records which is what we understand the case management judge was suggesting. 25 Another suggestion is that the respondent bear the initial cost of translating a random or representative sample of documents after which the case management judge would decide what documents appear to require immediate translation and what documents do not appear to need to be translated until further discovery demonstrates such need. 26 In order not to handcuff the case management judge and to confer upon him a proper measure of discretion, we have not crafted the aforesaid suggestions as directions of this Court. That said, it must be understood that should the case management judge adopt one or more of the suggestions and direct the parties accordingly, he will have done so with the approval of this panel. 27 In any event, we would expect that prior to fixing the amount of the security for the costs of translation, the case management judge scrutinize the translation costs the respondent incurs for their reasonableness. In other words, the amount of the security for costs may not necessarily be equal to the amount the respondent actually incurs by way of translation expenses. Such scrutiny would obviously mirror principles used to fix costs. For example, for the purpose of fixing the amount of the security required to be posted for the translation costs, the case management judge would determine whether it was reasonable to incur any particular translation cost. Was there a need to translate the document at all? If so, what level of translation was required? Finally, were the translation costs actually incurred reasonable in the sense that the translator's charges were not excessive having regard to the market cost of such translation?

sentences.text: Commentary § 5.7:1 Rule 5.7 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Describing Records In Dorchak v.
Krupka, 1997 ABCA 89, (sub nom.
Roy v.
Krilow) 196 A.R.
81 at pp.

84-94 [A.R.], Justice Côté discussed how to describe documents in an affidavit of records: The main issue here is how much detail an affidavit of documents must give about the individual documents which it discloses. . . . . .
In both affidavits of documents, the producible and the privileged documents are described the same way.
In each case, the description is very brief.
I will quote one: “Documents mechanically numbered 000001 to 000020.”… Each appellant swore an affidavit and submits that the numbering is sufficient description.
But each respondent (who sought the affidavit) seeks a detailed description of each individual document.
Each respondent apparently seeks a list giving the nature, date, name of author, and name of recipient, of each document. . . . . .

The cases seem to differ little respecting what are the basic principles The relevant Rules of Court are terse, and do not expressly call for much… These Rules establish discovery of documents, a valuable mechanism invented in Chancery centuries ago.
It is intended to prevent destruction or suppression of evidence, get admissions for trial, prevent surprise, and prevent fabrication of written or oral evidence.
An affidavit of documents must show unambiguously what documents' existence it does or does not disclose.
It must remove any uncertainty on the following vital question.
If a piece of paper turns up later, or is tendered on a motion or at trial, has it been disclosed by the previous affidavit of documents?
That question can arise in a motion for a further and better affidavit of documents, under rule 194(1).
It also arises when there is an objection to putting a document into evidence at trial, for failure to disclose it, under rule 195.
It is important that the affidavit remove any doubt on the topic … Either of the methods suggested by the opposing parties here would fill that bill.
If a document is in a bundle of individually numbered sheets, then it is easy to see from any the document's face and location that it is one of the documents disclosed [sic].

(If it is contended that it is an identical copy to a document produced, the one in the numbered bundle can be compared with it.) The numbering should be indelible, of course; pencilled numbers or flimsy tabs would not do: see Solid Waste v.
Philips, supra, at 487.
As our court said recently, such questions relate more to preservation than to discovery, and individual methods can be adapted in individual cases with different circumstances: Banque Nationale v.
Cdn.
Eng. & Surveys, supra.
The respondents' rival plan to describe each document separately without marking it is not quite so unambiguous; for example, there could be two different memos to file bearing the same date.
But it is probably good enough in most circumstances.
Besides that rule of unambiguous identification, does any other principle of justice or rule of law apply?
Where producible documents are concerned, I do not know of any.
It seems to me that everything else is just a matter of mechanics, convenience, and common sense. . . . . .
It is true that modern litigation management often benefits if each side in a complex suit prepares fairly detailed indexes of the truly important documents in the suit.
Sometimes a chronology of documents will reveal many interesting things, and give a good framework for oral discoveries.
But I see nothing in the Rules of Court or the decided cases saying that either lawyer must prepare such a tool for the other side.
Still less need a lawyer do so for all the marginally relevant documents which an affidavit of documents must disclose.
That is not the function of an affidavit of documents.
Indeed, such a finding tool prepared by one side would plainly be privileged.
If the two sides wish to eliminate duplication of effort by preparing such chronologies of important papers jointly, or by exchanging them, that is commendable.
But the present Rules and decided cases do nothing to compel such cooperation or exchange.
Banque Nationale de Paris (Can.) v.
Cdn.
Eng. & Surveys (Yukon), supra, involved millions of producible documents.
In that case, a list of hundreds of numbered bundles, with no other indication of their contents, would not have sufficed.
That would be even more true if the contents of the bundles were random, e.g. a company's files had been shuffled.
But in the Banque Nationale case, there was no problem, because a card index and other finding tools had been provided.
The courts held that sufficed.
I doubt that the index listed every single document, but where documents are grouped in some meaningful way, that is surely not necessary.
In a medium-sized suit, one often sees dozens of numbered bundles listed in the producible part of the affidavit of documents.
If the affidavit gives no indication whatever of their contents, and no other finding tool is provided, that is very likely not a good enough description.
It is not insufficient because it violates any particular rule of law, but simply because it is unworkable.
However, an affidavit listing such numbered bundles would suffice if its producible schedule briefly explained the basic nature or source of each bundle.
For example, it might say that one bundle contained the invoices and statements from the plaintiff to the defendant respecting the transactions and debts sued for.
And it might say that another bundle contained the plaintiff's Lethbridge branch's correspondence file for 1997 respecting the defendant.
And so forth.
The odd stray document which was important but did not fit logically into any bundle might need separate description.
What is an appropriate description or arrangement for a handful of producible documents may well not be appropriate for a roomful, and vice versa: Cdn.
Eng. & Surveys (Yuk.) v.
Banque Nationale de Paris (1995), 179 A.R.
(C.A.), supra.
What is a suitable mode of description or identification depends a good deal upon the circumstances of the individual case: G.W.L.
Properties Ltd. et al. v.
Grace (W.R.) & Co.-Conn.
S.C.); leave denied (1993), 22 B.C.A.C.
78 (C.A.) … Our court has already rejected any rule which requires that individual documents always be individually listed: Banque Nationale v.
Cdn.
Eng., supra. . . . . .
The orthodox law is all digested by Chitty in a detailed article in, [1924] 2 D.L.R.
The cases reported to then uniformly permit numbered bundles without lists of individual documents.
Many of the later cases cite or quote Chitty's review with approval.
Many cases on this topic cite Visa Internaltional Service Association v.
Block Brothers Realty Ltd., [1983] 4 W.W.R.
S.C.); affd.
That case expressly permits producible documents to be discovered in bundles of similar sorts of papers, without individually listing the papers.
(The Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal, which had nothing to do with producible documents: (1983), 64 B.C.L.R.

(2d) 390.) In modern complex litigation with large numbers of producible documents, it is certainly permissible to group them into bundles or groups with common characteristics, and to describe the groups without itemizing individual documents: G.W.L.
Props. v.
W.R.
Grace, supra.

For all these reasons, I cannot agree that the appellants need have listed and described the producible documents individually, if it was convenient to number them mechanically and treat them as a group. . . . . .

Such a long list is totally unworkable… But if instead the affidavit lists correspondence files by subject or time period or office, and lists bundles of other documents such as invoices or reports by type and age, then almost any document can readily be located.
Even thousands of producible documents can be sensibly described and readily found in a two-page list of a few dozen numbered bundles of similar papers arranged by topic.
Such a list takes under a minute to read.
For that reason, the English courts have consistently held that a large number of producible documents must be arranged by characteristics and described by numbered bundles.
They must not be individually described in a bulky inventory; such a fat list of individual documents is an abuse of process: Walker v.
Poole (1882), 21 Ch.
D.
835; Hill v.
Hart-Davis (1884), 26 Ch.
D.
If long individual lists were too awkward and slow in that more leisurely gaslit age, they are an abomination in today's more congested courts.
In accord is G.W.L. v.
W.A.
Grace, supra.
This court recently refused to order such individual listing of producible documents, in a large suit, in Banque Nationale v.
Cdn.
Eng. & Surveys, supra.
It doubted that there was even a presumption in favour of listing documents individually. . . . . .
Now I will turn to the privileged documents.
Here also, the first principle is seeing whether one can unequivocally say of a given piece of paper whether its existence has been disclosed in the affidavit or not.
And many of the questions of convenience are broadly similar.
Here again, a numbered bundle fills the bill at least as well as individual descriptions.
But privilege imports a second principle of law.
Privilege is an important substantive rule of law, not to be frittered away: Descoteaux et al. v.
Mierzwinski et al., [1982] 1 S.C.R.
860 … Therefore, it is beside the point to speak of the modern tendency to widen discovery, or to imply that privilege is old-fashioned: those fallacies are demolished in Hodgkinson v.
(2d) 129, 134–36 (C.A.) … Any system of listing or describing privileged documents which gives away privileged information is therefore unthinkable.
There is considerable danger of giving away secrets by describing the individual privileged documents: see London & Midland General Insurance Co. v.
Lambert, [1972] 1 W.W.R.
224 (Alta.
Dist.
Ct.) 226, and cases there cited… . . . . .
Furthermore, in this age of photocopying and e-mail, people rarely write out long recitals.
They write short letters or memos, and attach relevant existing documents.
To force a person to list what documents were attached to a privileged document would often be to reveal virtually all the contents of the privileged communication.
To describe a document as a blueprint, an X- ray, a tracing or log from certain scientific apparatus, or as a videotape or a tape recording, often will give away the whole secret.
The danger of giving away privileged secrets means that the description of the privileged documents need not include dates, contents, or parties to them: Curlett v.
Canadian Fire Insurance Co.
(No.
Cf.
London & Midland v.
Lambert, supra.
I reiterate that such individual details are not necessary to prove whether the existence of a given privileged document is revealed by the affidavit of documents.
A bundle of numbered papers suffices.
Indeed, because consecutive document numbers are unambiguous, they are slightly better for that purpose than word descriptions of individual documents: see Solid Waste v.
Philip, supra.
One must not apply uncritically to privileged documents reported cases involving only producible documents, such as G.W.L. v.
W.A.
Grace, supra, or Cdn.
Eng. & Surveys v.
Banque Nationale de Paris, supra.
As noted, cases on producible documents depend largely on convenience, not law.
And revealing information about producible documents is good, subject to expense and convenience.
But revealing information about privileged documents is dangerous.

Occasionally one will find a decided case suggesting briefly that the description of individual privileged documents in an affidavit of documents must be full enough to let the court or the opponent assess whether privilege is properly claimed in respect of each document… In my view, that suggestion of law is wrong.
The description of the documents in the schedule need not corroborate privilege… . . . . .
I would not follow Creaser v.
Warren (1987), 77 N.S.R.
It required that the affidavit set out the status of the sender and recipient of each document said to be privileged…Creaser is distinguishable.
It simply applies a Nova Scotia Rule of Court which expressly calls for a “description of each document”.
Alberta's Rules contain no such requirement… . . . . .
So ordinarily it is sufficient for the affidavit's second part of the first schedule to list and describe privileged documents merely as numbered bundles.
Details of individual documents are unnecessary… . . . . .
I do not wish to leave the impression that it would suffice merely to describe the privileged papers in a big suit as “5287 sheets numbered in red 1 to 5287”.
One would expect some kind of identification of the bundles in a bigger suit… It is a question of practicality.
For example, papers generated by counsel for the purpose of this suit after it existed or was contemplated are plainly privileged.
There is no reason not to say one bundle is counsel's file.
Indeed saying so might avoid a lot of suspicion, requests that the court examine the documents under rule 194, and so forth.
Ordinarily one should be able to describe a file or bundle in some manner which will not reveal secrets.
For example … one may call it a lawyer's file without naming the lawyer. . . . . .

Quite aside from a list of mechanically numbered papers, the list of privileged documents in the Schedule of each affidavit contains a second item in these words: Documents, correspondence, memoranda, briefs, communications, proofs, working-papers, photographs, plans, diagrams and miscellaneous documents forming Counsel's brief. … This is a mere vague reference to correspondence with solicitors or to documents for litigation… It is completely insufficient, if there are no numbered bundles or other description.

How could one ever later tell whether a given paper was one of the documents which had been referred to so vague and generic a way? … Up to this point, the topic has been how to describe the documents now (or formerly) in the party's possession or power.
A completely different topic is what reasons for any claim of privilege in the body of the affidavit of documents.

Rule 188(b) says: The affidavit … shall state … the party objects to produce and the grounds for any such objection, … The reasons must be fairly precise, and must recite enough facts to trigger privilege.
For example, if the body of the affidavit refers to three kinds of privilege (solicitor's advice, litigation, and without-prejudice), it should indicate which papers fall within which.
Nor is it enough to speak of communications with a solicitor; one must swear that they were for the purpose of getting advice.
Nor is it enough to say that papers were for the purpose of resisting a claim; one must also say they were created when the claim existed or was contemplated.
Here each affidavit refers to at least two different types of privilege, and does not say which paper falls within which category: I object to produce the said documents on the following grounds:
(a) Material obtained for or by Counsel in contemplation of litigation; and

(b) Privileged professional communications of a confidential character passing between Counsel, third parties and Client for the purpose of giving and taking legal advice and arising in contemplation of litigation.
That will not do.
The individual types of privilege must be segregated, and the affidavit must say which numbered documents come within each type of privilege.
Madam Justice Veit, in Canadian Engineering & Surveys (Yukon) Ltd. v.
Banque Nationale de Paris (Canada) (1995), 179 A.R.
394 (Q.B.), said at p.
395: Where a large number of documents is subject to discovery, those documents need not be individually listed and described.
Her Ladyship then listed the principles to be applied when disclosing records.
At p.

[19] Justice Côté went on to observe at para 16 that where “documents are grouped in some meaningful way” an index listing every single document is not necessary.

He held at para 18 that “an affidavit listing such numbered bundles would suffice if its producible schedule briefly explained the basic nature or source of each bundle.” Dorchak appears to permit bundling records of the same nature or from the same source.
[20] Following Dorchak, a new version of the Rules was adopted.

Rule 5.7 modifies the law discussed in Dorchak. … [21] The practice of bundling records is justified in Dorchak partly on the basis that sometimes, in cases with a large volume of records, it is too laborious to describe each individual record.

This reality has been overtaken in most large-scale litigation by what is referred to as e-Discovery, in which document production is often outsourced to specialized service providers who make extensive use of technology including Artificial Intelligence (AI).
In cases where record numbering and descriptions are generated by a computer, saving labour does not provide much justification for bundling.
[22] Today, bundling is most often seen in cases like the present one, where a party is required to produce hard copy records and is financially strapped.
Ms.
Hami, a legal assistant working for counsel for the Defendants, deposed that record production was hampered by the Defendants' lack of funds.
Bundling, though often sub-optimal for the efficient resolution of disputes, is a justifiable expedient for under-resourced litigants.
With that said, Courts must be alive to the potential abuse of the practice of bundling by recalcitrant litigants who use bundling as a strategy to conceal records and obstruct their adversaries. ….
[26] The adequacy of the descriptions provided is inextricably intertwined with the next question, which is whether the bundled records are “all of the same nature” as required by Rule 5.7(2)(a).
There is no judicial consideration of the meaning of the term “of the same nature” in Alberta or in the other provinces and Federal Court where the same prerequisite to bundling exists.

[27] The “same nature” requirement was adopted as a corrective to Dorchak which was viewed by the civil litigation bar as allowing over-bundling that “leads to cross-examinations on affidavits and prolongs examinations for discovery”: Alberta Law Reform Institute, Alberta Rules of Court Project: Document Discovery and Examination for Discovery, Consultation Memorandum No.
12.2 (October 2002) at 27.
The ALRI report at page 29 recommended the adoption of the “same nature” concept from the Federal Court Rules though without any explanation of what the idea meant.
All that can be taken from the ALRI report is that “same nature” was intended to be more restrictive than the “meaningful grouping” concept in Dorchak.

[28] A textual reading of Rule 5.7(2) also suggests that “same nature” is a narrower concept than “meaningful grouping.” Records of a different nature – for example, an agreement and a photograph – may be gathered in a meaningful grouping if there is some other logic that connects the records.
The Plaintiffs argued that records of the same nature means that they are the same type or class of record and should be from a defined period.

For example, an appropriate bundle would be “Statements for CIBC Account 1234-56789 for 2022.” Another example of an appropriate bundle would be “Invoices Issued by XYZ Corp in January 2023.” Even in some situations it may be appropriate to bundle hard copy correspondence as, for example, “Correspondence Received by A.B.C. from September 1, 2021 to December 31, 2021.” Such bundles can be succinctly described, are an efficient way to produce records for the producing party, and do not compromise the receiving party's ability to understand what is being produced.
Such an approach is efficient and consistent with the purpose and intention of the Rules as stated in Rule 1.2.
[29] The Plaintiffs submit that Rule 5.7 should be interpreted consistent with its text and with a pragmatic and functional understanding of the record production process.

Records of the “same nature” (i.e. homogeneous) can efficiently be “described in sufficient detail to enable another party to understand what it contains” whereas a bundle of disparate records (i.e. heterogeneous) requires a comprehensive description of the contents of the bundle to achieve the same effect. ….
[31] Given the longstanding practice in Alberta, reflected in Dorchak and Blough [Blough v.
Busy Music Inc.

2018 ABQB 560], of bundling records received from a common source, I cannot read “same nature” as to restrict the practice of bundling only to situations where there is the same type or class of record such as bank statements or invoices.
Records from a common source may be of the same nature, particularly where, as in the present case, there are other characteristics identified that connect the bundled records.
Such an interpretation also maintains the flexibility that bundling provides for parties that are financially constrained.
[32] Though the disputed records may be bundled, that does not end the analysis.

Rule 5.7(2)(b) imposes a duty on the disclosing party to describe the bundle “in sufficient detail to enable another party to understand what it contains.” The approach to describing bundles must be adjusted depending on the context; the principle of proportionality that governs record production applies to the description of bundles.
Where a bundle is comprised of homogeneous records (e.g. bank statements from a single account for a defined period) a terse description is all that is needed.
The more heterogeneous the contents of a bundle, the more robust the description required.
This is an example of what Justice Marion, writing about a different aspect of record production, called “common sense and proportionality”: MBH v CKI, 2023 ABKB 284 at para 40.
