ShawCor Ltd., 2014 ABCA 289, 2014 CarswellAlta 1582, 580 A.R.
265, 2 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 581, the Court of Appeal gave direction on how to describe in an affidavit of records those documents over which privilege is claimed.

At paragraphs 8-9, 36, 41, 50-51, 72-73, and 92, the Court said: 8 We have concluded that a party preparing an affidavit of records must, short of revealing information that is privileged, provide a sufficient description of each record for which privilege is claimed to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege.

While the objective is to reduce the need for parties to seek recourse to other time-consuming and costly litigation steps, we are equally satisfied that this can be accomplished in a manner that does not injure valid privileges.

In addition, where a judge is nevertheless called on to determine privilege issues, a sufficient description of records will assist the judge in determining whether a more probing assessment is required and, if so, the confines of that assessment.
9 This result is premised on a number of specific conclusions.
Rule 5.7 was intended to apply to all relevant and material records, even those a party objects to produce.
Thus, in an affidavit of records, a party must number all records in a convenient manner and briefly describe them (Rule 5.7(1)).
The right to bundle and treat that bundle as a single record under Rule 5.7(2) applies equally to records over which privilege is claimed.
Rule 5.8 imposes additional responsibilities on a party who objects to produce a prima facie producible record.
The particular ground(s) of the objection must be identified with respect to each record in order to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege.

That means the party must state the actual privilege being relied upon with respect to that record and describe the record in a way that, without revealing information that is privileged, indicates how the record fits within the claimed privilege.
These requirements apply equally to a bundled record over which a party claims privilege. … 36 Rules 5.6, 5.7 and 5.8 lie at the heart of this dispute.

As noted above, we have concluded that a grammatical, purposive and contextual reading of these Rules imposes on a party the obligation to number and briefly describe each record that is relevant and material, including those it claims are privileged.
In accordance with Schedule 2 of Form 26, those latter records should be set out in separate categories as contemplated therein.
A party is entitled to bundle privileged records providing that the bundled record otherwise meets the requirements of Rule 5.7.

For records that a party claims are privileged, the party must, in accordance with Rule 5.8, identify the particular grounds of the objection to production for each record in order to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege.

That means the party must state the actual privilege being relied upon with respect to that record and describe the record in a way that, without revealing information that is privileged, indicates how the record fits within the claimed privilege.

These requirements apply equally to a bundled record over which a party claims privilege. … … [41] It follows that we do not view Rules 5.7 and 5.8 as creating discrete obligations and rights depending on whether a party objects to produce records.

Rather, despite any ambiguity suggested by their headings, we are satisfied that Rule 5.7 was intended to apply to all relevant and material records that are prima facie producible and that Rule 5.8 was intended to impose additional, not separate, obligations on a party who objects to producing a prima facie producible record.
What further information does Rule 5.8 require a party to disclose for records over which privilege is claimed?

The answer is that it requires, in particular, that a party identify the “grounds for the objection in respect of each record”. … [50] As noted, we have concluded that each record over which privilege is claimed must be
(i) numbered in a convenient order and
(ii) described in a way that, without revealing privileged information, indicates how that record fits within the claimed privilege.

However, this requirement to describe each record individually is subject to the proviso that relevant and material records of the same nature can be bundled and treated as a single record so long as the requirements of Rule 5.7(2) are met.
That is, the description offered for the bundle must be sufficiently clear so as to allow another party to understand what it contains.

In addition, given the requirements of Rule 5.8, this description must also provide sufficient facts to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege over the bundle in question.
[51] Bundling can be effective even with multiple claims of privilege.
To illustrate, consider a party who claims privilege over 50 records.

After describing the bundle in sufficient detail to enable another party to understand what it contains and providing sufficient information to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege over the bundle in question, the party objecting to disclosure identifies records 1 to 30 as subject to solicitor-client privilege, records 40 to 50 as litigation privilege and records 31 to 39 as both.

This permits a party to identify which form(s) of privilege attaches to each record while recognizing that some records might have multiple reasons for objection, any one of which may be sufficient: see Opron Construction Co. v Alberta
(1989), 1989 ABCA 279 (CanLII), 100 AR 58 (CA) at para 5.
Another party would be assisted by this degree of specificity and might well choose to accept the objections, or only resist them selectively.

A judge reviewing the records under Rule 5.11 would also be in a better position to organize the evaluation of the objections. … [72] In summary, records where privilege is asserted must now be dealt with individually.
Each record must be numbered in a convenient order and briefly described, short of disclosing privileged information.
Records may be bundled where privilege is being asserted providing that the bundled record otherwise meets the requirements of Rule 5.7.
In accordance with Rule 5.8, a party must also identify the grounds for claiming privilege with respect to each record in order to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claim.

This latter requirement means that, for each record, a party must state the particular privilege being asserted and describe the record in a way, again without revealing information that is privileged, that indicates how the record fits within the claimed privilege.
The description of all relevant and material records over which privilege is claimed should be set out in Schedule 2 of Form 26 in the separate categories contemplated therein.
[73] CNRL's affidavits do not comply with these requirements.

Harvey's first affidavit made a blanket claim of privilege over an undisclosed number of documents and merely listed the privilege categories set out in Schedule 2 of Form 26, with nothing added except the word “NIL” in reference to the “Other” category.

While Harvey's later affidavit disclosed the number of records over which privilege was claimed, namely 1,058, and stated that these records fell into five discrete categories, this too falls well short of what is required under the Rules.
It follows that the appeal must be allowed.

CNRL is directed to prepare a new or supplementary affidavit in compliance with the Rules and this judgment. … [92] Without limiting what we have said, we summarize for convenience the requirements of the Rules discussed above relating to affidavits of records and privilege claims.
We stress that this is not intended to be an exhaustive list of those requirements: 1.
Every relevant and material record is prima facie producible and the minimum requirements and rights under Rule 5.7(1) and
(2) apply to all such records, even where a party objects to production based on claimed privilege or some other legal ground.
Every relevant and material record must be numbered in a convenient order and briefly described.
These should be set out in the separate Schedules applicable to each as contemplated in Form 26.
Accordingly, a party claiming privilege over a number of records must number and briefly describe each record short of revealing information that is privileged.
The description of those records should be set out in Schedule 2 of Form 26 in the separate categories contemplated therein.

A party is permitted to bundle and treat as a single record a group of records that are all of the same nature so long as the bundle is, in accordance with Rule 5.7(2)(b), described in sufficient detail to enable another party to understand what it contains.
This bundling option also applies to records over which a party claims privilege.

If a party objects to the disclosure of otherwise relevant and material records, it shall, in addition to numbering the records in a convenient order and briefly describing them, set forth the grounds for objection in respect of each record to assist other parties in assessing the validity of the claimed privilege.
In doing so, the party is required to
(i) state the actual privilege being relied upon with respect to that record; and
(ii) describe the record in a way that, without revealing privileged information, indicates how the record fits within the claimed privilege.
These requirements also apply to a bundled record over which a party claims privilege.

Making a blanket assertion that both forms of privilege apply, in instances where one or the other is clearly unavailable, is a litigation tactic that ought to be discouraged.
46 Parties must describe the documents in a way that indicates the basis for their claim: ShawCor at para 9.
The grounds for claiming solicitor-client privilege and litigation privilege are distinct.
A description that supports one class of privilege does not necessarily support the other.

47 To support a claim of solicitor-client privilege, Suncor must at least describe the documents in a manner that indicates communications between a client and a legal advisor related to seeking or receiving legal advice.
48 To support a claim of litigation privilege, Suncor must describe documents with enough particularity to indicate whether the dominant purpose for their creation was in contemplation of litigation.

It is not disputed that solicitor and client privilege is one of the most carefully guarded principles of our legal system: Canada (Privacy Commissioner) v Blood Tribe Department of Health, 2008 SCC 44 at para.

44, 120; University of Calgary v JR, 2015 ABCA 118 at para.

20 The appellants and the Law Society argue that i) the Master's order compromises the privilege over the files; ii) the files are third party records and should only be obtained using the procedure under R 5.13; and iii) the Master's order was made without notice being given to the clients.
21 The Rules on the production of records recognize that privilege may be asserted over some records, and specifically deal with the issue.
As noted, the Rules draw a distinction between the “disclosure” of records and the subsequent “production” of records.
Under R.
5.6 a party must “disclose all records”, or in other words must make a list of them all.
Rule 5.6(2)(b) recognizes that there may be valid objections to “producing” certain records, but still requires the litigants to “disclose” or list them.
Rule 5.8 confirms that if a party objects to production of any records, they must still be identified in some suitable manner, and disclosed.

22 The concerns of the appellants and the Law Society are addressed by the structure of the Rules.
The Master did not order the production of any records, only their disclosure or listing.
The Master specifically declined (at para.
33) to consider any issue of privilege, recognizing that the review of the claim for privilege under R.
5.11(1)(b) would follow later.
The formal order specifically states that issues of privilege are left for future consideration.

41-2, 366 DLR (4th) 169, argued and reserved SCC #35590.
That may be so, but the Rules of Court nevertheless require that they be disclosed, even if not eventually produced because of a valid claim of privilege.
Exceptions to solicitor and client privilege are not easily recognized, but when an enactment specifically calls for disclosure, the enactment prevails.

The chambers judge modified the Master's order to the extent of allowing the files to be disclosed anonymously, a modification which effectively mitigated any objection that might be made on this ground.
24 Thus the appellants' arguments about breaches of privilege are premature.

5.13 makes little difference if the clients are given notice either way.
25 There is a chicken-and-egg aspect to the appellants' position.
The respondents do not want to see or review every file in the offices of the defendant lawyers.
They are only interested in real estate files involving the same alleged main fraudster and bank loans officer.
If the respondents were really required to proceed under R.

5.13 relating to the production of documents of third parties, and if they could only proceed on notice to the other straw buyer clients, how would they know which clients to serve with the application?
If they are not entitled to a list of the relevant records, they would be forced to give notice to every client of the lawyers.
Under the Master's order, there will be a discrete target list of clients who have files that are said to be within the scope of relevance.

This is undoubtedly why the Rules require that even privileged documents be listed, with issues of production and privilege deferred until later. … 38 The Law Society also notes that its Code of Conduct places an obligation on a lawyer to protect the confidentiality of the client's files.

32, 29 Alta LR (5th) 37, 482 AR 136; D. v National Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Children, [1978] AC 171 at pp.

Div.), wherein Kitely J. held that correspondence and other written materials relevant to the issue of confusion between two trademarks in foreign countries should be produced, and further noted, at para.46, “There is no obligation on the party producing the documents to translate them into English; that will be the responsibility of the party who leads the evidence at trial.” Similarly, in Bilfinger Berger (Canada) Inc. v.

On the other hand, Rule 5.6(1) provides that an affidavit of records must disclose all relevant and material records.

The latter documents will clearly have to be translated.

The Court then made these additional suggestions (paragraphs 23–27): 23 While we are loathe to interfere with the case management judge's management of this case, we are concerned about the number of Turkish documents disclosed and the consequences of having either party bear the cost of translating them.
So, we would suggest that the appellant be given the opportunity to produce a further and better affidavit of records after a further review of its documents.
In oral argument, it was suggested that there may have been considerable duplication in the appellant's production.
It is perhaps also the case that, out of an abundance of caution, more documents were produced than necessary.
It may be that some of the 25,000 Turkish documents produced are not relevant or material and therefore do not require translation.
Now knowing that it might have to bear the cost of translating some or all of the documents it disclosed, the appellant may wish an opportunity to revisit its affidavit of records.
A culling of production could reduce the amount of translation required and correspondingly the quantum of security that need be posted.

24 If reducing the number of documents disclosed is not possible, the appellant might be given the opportunity to assist the respondent in understanding what documents it produced in its affidavit of records which is what we understand the case management judge was suggesting.

25 Another suggestion is that the respondent bear the initial cost of translating a random or representative sample of documents after which the case management judge would decide what documents appear to require immediate translation and what documents do not appear to need to be translated until further discovery demonstrates such need.
26 In order not to handcuff the case management judge and to confer upon him a proper measure of discretion, we have not crafted the aforesaid suggestions as directions of this Court.
That said, it must be understood that should the case management judge adopt one or more of the suggestions and direct the parties accordingly, he will have done so with the approval of this panel.

27 In any event, we would expect that prior to fixing the amount of the security for the costs of translation, the case management judge scrutinize the translation costs the respondent incurs for their reasonableness.
In other words, the amount of the security for costs may not necessarily be equal to the amount the respondent actually incurs by way of translation expenses.
Such scrutiny would obviously mirror principles used to fix costs.

For example, for the purpose of fixing the amount of the security required to be posted for the translation costs, the case management judge would determine whether it was reasonable to incur any particular translation cost.
Was there a need to translate the document at all?
If so, what level of translation was required?
Finally, were the translation costs actually incurred reasonable in the sense that the translator's charges were not excessive having regard to the market cost of such translation?

sentences.text: Producible records for which there is an objection to produce

paragraphs.text: (1) Subject to subrules (3) to (5), for each producible record that a party objects to produce, the affidavit of records must (a) number the record in a convenient order, and (b) describe the grounds for the objection to produce the record. (2) For the purposes of this rule, the description in the affidavit of records of any record the party objects to produce and the grounds for the objection must be sufficient to enable a court reviewing the records to confirm that each record is disclosed in the affidavit without undermining or proving the privilege that is claimed in respect of the records. (3) Subject to subrule (4), if a party objects to produce a number of related records on the same grounds, the records may be bundled and numbered, and the records along with the grounds for the objection to produce the records may be collectively described in the affidavit of records. (4) For greater certainty, (a) producible records that a party objects to produce that are in the files of a lawyer (i) may be disclosed collectively in the affidavit of records without being numbered, if the records consist of the lawyer's work product, including working notes and memoranda prepared by the lawyer or the law firm and communications with the client and opposing counsel, (ii) may be numbered or bundled and may be disclosed collectively in the affidavit of records, if the records are described in a manner that distinguishes (A) records for which solicitor and client privilege is claimed, (B) records that were prepared for the dominant purpose of litigation, and (C) records for which production is objected to on a ground other than those referred to in paragraphs (A) and (B), and (b) producible records that a party does not object to produce that are in the files of a lawyer must be separately disclosed in the affidavit of records. (5) Expert reports prepared for the dominant purpose of litigation, and records related to those expert reports, must be disclosed in accordance with rule 5.35, and not in accordance with this Division. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.10:1 Rule 5.10 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.10. 1. Who Bears the Cost? Generally the person with “power or custody” of the records will bear the cost of their production. The plaintiff's action is for dental malpractice. Certain undertakings were given in connection with the production of documents relative to subsequent treatment by other professionals. Counsel for the plaintiff has acknowledged that the requested documents are relevant but has objected to their production solely on the basis that as they are required by the defendants, the defendants should bear the cost of their production… The respondent's objection raises the question of whether a document is in a party's “power” if he must pay for it before it is produced… A party's power over a document is that party's entitlement to obtain the document or a copy of it. The fact that there is a cost in obtaining it is irrelevant. To hold otherwise would permit parties to avoid production of relevant documents on the basis of cost. As was stated by an Ontario Master in Hathway v. Bond (1986), 11 C.P.C. (2d) 277 at 280: It is a principle of our system of litigation that each party bears the expense of conducting his or her own case and the successful party is usually reimbursed in whole or in part for these costs. In an annotation to Schultz v. Galvin, supra, Lawrence Theall prefers the reasons in Hathway v. Bond on the basis … Therefore, the fact that some cost is involved in fulfilling an obligation should not be the basis upon which a party may avoid such an obligation. There are significant costs related in meeting other obligations under the Rules. A party must pay their solicitors for the cost of reviewing and organizing documents for production and preparing the affidavit of documents. The same reasoning should also apply to documents which are in a party's control. Where the person is not ‘entitled’ to a document but the document may still be obtained for a cost, it is submitted the document should still be considered to be in a person's ‘control’. The Manitoba Court of Queen's Bench in Royal Bank v. Waller (1991), 74 Man. R. (2d) 32, adopts the same position [p. 34]: After reviewing the decisions and considering the arguments of counsel, I have come to the conclusion that normally a party required to produce information should bear the cost of so doing. It is trite to observe that the philosophy pertaining to discovery has broadened over the years and that the more expansive approach has been embodied in the new Queen's Bench Rules. As already noted, the obligation to produce or provide answers is not in issue. The fact that there is a cost attendant upon a party discharging its obligations should not be permitted to defeat the policy of the Rules, unless, on the particular facts of a case, it can be established that the information sought is of such little relevance or the cost of producing it so unreasonably high that the burden should be shifted onto the party seeking the information. There will always be some cost attached to the discovery process, be it in researching answers or obtaining documents. Extra staff assistance, professional help, photocopying or other disbursements will be incurred. Those expenses should be considered at the end of the litigation process in the course of assessing costs. They should not be an excuse for curtailing discovery or production. If Mr. Douglas still acted for Waller, and if additional fees were charged by him as a result of effort expended during the discovery process, that expense or the exposure to that expense could not be a justification for refusing to answer legitimate questions or to providing compellable documents. The same could be said when the assistance of an auditor or a party's own employee is required. Having concluded that the fact that some cost is involved in fulfilling an obligation should not be a basis upon which a party can avoid discharging its obligation, it follows that in the circumstances of this particular case the learned Master erred when he made his order against Waller conditional upon the payment by the Royal Bank of Canada of Mr. Douglas' account. The appeal is therefore allowed with costs. The same conclusion was arrived at by Master Quinn in Van Der Ploeg v. Quick (1983), 27 Alta. L.R. (2d) 221 at 222: Upon perusing the file in these proceedings, I note that there has been no affidavit of documents demanded by the defendant. Until a demand has been made by the defendant and an affidavit filed by the plaintiff which refers to the documents in question there is no basis upon which the defendant can demand production of the documents for inspection. When such a demand has been made and an affidavit of documents has been filed referring to the aforesaid documents, the plaintiff will be obligated to produce the documents (or, in this case, possibly photocopies of same) for the inspection of the defendants. There is nothing in the rules which indicates that such an order would be made conditional upon the party seeking inspection to pay any disbursements required in connection with the production of the documents for inspection. It seems clear that such disbursements would become costs in the cause. I am not, however, prepared to state that the rule is without exception. In circumstances where a plaintiff is impoverished and has an action which sounds well founded the Court might extend the same principles governing a security for costs application to the production of documents. The logic in cases such a Vollenga v. Berry (1962), 39 W.W.R. 319 (Alta. C.A.), and Proniuk v. Petryk, [1933] 1 W.W.R. 648; affirmed [1935] 3 W.W.R. 223 (Alta. C.A.), might in appropriate circumstances be extended to this type of application. Labrosse v. Eli Markovitch Professional Corp. (1993), 14 Alta. L.R. (3d) 204 (Master), at 205-208, per Master Waller. 2. Possession of Records by Others Possession of the records by persons other than the party is irrelevant. First, the fact that others might also have copies of documents is irrelevant. The rules require a litigant who has documents in his possession or power relating to matters or questions in the action be produced. It is not an answer for a litigant to say “Joe also has copies of the documents. Get them from him.”Gauthier v. Alberta Recoveries & Rentals Ltd. (1993), 21 C.P.C. (3d) 193 (Master), at 196, per Master Funduk. 3. Records Created Other than in Course of Duty Records which are created voluntarily are not different from those created pursuant to duty. … the fact that these tests and documents were done voluntarily by the Crown employee (not in the course of her duties) is irrelevant. Lots of documents are created voluntarily. That is not the test for production of documents. Gauthier v. Alberta Recoveries & Rentals Ltd. (1993), 21 C.P.C. (3d) 193 (Master), at 197, per Master Funduk.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.11:1 Rule 5.11 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.11. 1. Inspection of Records by the Court In Enerflow Industries Inc. v. NOV Enerflow ULC, 2017 ABQB 334, 2017 CarswellAlta 852, 55 Alta. L.R. (6th) 200, Justice McCarthy discussed the provision of R. 5.11 which permits a Court to inspect the records sought to be produced. His Lordship said: 7 While Rule 5.11 provides the court with discretion to inspect a record over which privilege is claimed, this discretion ought to be exercised sparingly (Canadian Natural at paras 64-65) [Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. ShawCor Ltd. 2014 ABCA 289]: It is true that the right to have a judge review records claimed to be privileged remains the ultimate safeguard in the event of legitimate differences of opinion or allegations of abuse of the system. But it is preferable that the Rules be interpreted in a way that minimizes the need to pursue these other various options, all of which come at additional cost and time to the litigants. Full and fair discovery of records also militates in favour of earlier dispute resolution and enhances the likelihood that opposing parties will make only appropriate challenges. Further, in this day of increasingly scarce judicial resources, judges should not be bogged down regularly by the need to examine volumes of records to assess privilege. And lawyers should not be put in the position of having to ask them to do so. This potential Hobson's choice can be avoided by a system of document discovery that requires a brief description of each record claimed to be privileged in the affidavit of records. Providing that description at an early stage will help counsel focus and, in many cases, resolve litigation privilege issues without their being required to shoot all the arrows in the litigation quiver. Many privilege claims will no doubt be readily accepted. It also means that where court review is still required, a judge will not likely be called on to examine every record subject to a privilege claim. And even if that should prove necessary, a brief description of the challenged records may well also save judicial time. 8 In Keefer Laundry Ltd v Pellerin Milnor Corp, 2006 BCSC 1180, a case relied on by the Applicants, the Court reluctantly reviewed 18 documents to determine whether privilege was properly made noting, however, that “it is preferable to resolve disputes over whether documents are privileged on the basis of affidavits rather than review of the document by the court” because: first, it ensures an open process, and second, the court will often not be in the position to know facts that should be known and necessary to assess whether privilege applies, such as who the people are who are named as sending and receiving emails (at paras 74–76). 9 The Applicant relies on TransAlta Corporation v Market Surveillance Administrator, 2015 ABQB 180 as authority for their argument that the Court ought to review the contested records. In that case, however, the Court of Appeal directed this Court to determine whether privilege was properly claimed according to the procedure to deal with contested privilege claims set out in s. 50 of the Alberta Utilities Commission Act, SA 2007, c A-37.2 (at para 5, see also 2014 ABCA 196). TransAlta should not be held out as an example of a common procedure, rather it appears to be an exception based on the particular circumstances of that case. 10 In summary, it is not “common practice”, as the Applicants suggest, for the Court to review documents to determine whether a privilege claim is proper, rather it is a discretionary decision for the Court, and one that ought to be exercised sparingly. It is preferable to assess a privilege claim on the basis of admissible affidavit evidence when available. The next issue, then, is whether the affidavit evidence of the Respondents' corporate representative is admissible. In AARC Society v. Sparks, 2018 ABCA 177, 2018 CarswellAlta 901, 71 Alta. L.R. (6th) 83, 19 C.P.C. (8th) 254, the Court discussed the evidentiary foundation which must exist before a court will inspect documents for which privilege is claimed. 5 Before a court orders the inspection of allegedly privileged communications there must be a sufficient evidentiary basis to support an inference that may justify the exception to solicitor-client privilege. The applicant must show prima facie evidence that those communications were made in furtherance of, or to facilitate, the client's own misconduct: see Scott & Associates Engineering Ltd v Ghost Pine Windfarm, LP, 2011 ABQB 339 at para 41, 520 AR 173. The following passage from O'Rourke v Darbishire and Others, [1920] UKHL 730, 57 SLR 730 at 732 aptly summarizes what is required before the court will exercise its discretion to inspect records: [T]here must be in order to get rid of privilege, not merely an allegation that they [communications over which privilege is asserted] were made for the purpose of getting advice for the commission of a fraud, but there must be something to give colour to the charge. The statement must be made in clear and definite terms, and there must further be some prima facie evidence that it has some foundation in fact. It is with reference to cases of this kind that it can be correctly said that the Court has a discretion as to ordering inspection of documents. It is obvious that it would be absurd to say that the privilege could be got rid of merely by making a charge of fraud. The Court will exercise its discretion not merely as to the terms in which the allegation is made, but also as to the surrounding circumstances, for the purposes of seeing whether the charge is made honestly and with sufficient probability of its truth to make it right to disallow the privilege of professional communication. 2. Opposing Counsel Not Allowed to Inspect Alberta R. 5(e) deals with “court”. It includes a judge sitting in chambers inspecting documents. It does not include counsel to the parties before him. Perhaps it should. This is an application under R. 194(2) [now R. 5.11] for inspection of an opposing party's documents. Nothing in the Rule as it is framed contemplates release of the documents, whose production is disputed under a claim of public interest immunity, to opposing counsel on his promise never to reveal what they contain. Pocklington Foods Inc. v. Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) (1993), 8 Alta. L.R. (3d) 429 (C.A.), at 441, per McClung J.A. 3. Any relevant evidence can be used to show that the affidavit of records is deficient In Questor Technology Inc. v. Stagg, 2021 ABQB 636, 2021 CarswellAlta 1933, Mr. Justice Nixon said: [46] In making this determination, I acknowledge the Defendants argued that the sole purpose of a cross-examination on an affidavit of records is to test the accuracy of the affidavit: 694994 Alberta Ltd v Fort McKay Metis Corp, 2001 ABQB 424 at para 4 (Master Funduk) [Fort McKay Metis]. However, a cross-examination is not the only method by which an affidavit of records can be shown to be inaccurate. In my view, a party can rely on any relevant evidence to support an assertion that an affidavit of records many have omitted documents: Re/Max Real Estate (Edmonton) Ltd v Border Credit Union Ltd, [1988] 6 WWR 146, 1988 CanLII 3489 at paras 1, 21. 4. Redactions In MBH v. CKI, 2023 ABKB 284, 2023 CarswellAlta 1221, Justice Marion discussed the redaction of records, and the approach a court should take when faced with an application to order the production of redacted records: [35] The issue here, then, is when the court should order disclosure of redacted records that are provided in the context of a questioning on an affidavit. In the context of Part 5 disclosure under the Rules, rule 5.11 allows courts to compel the production of a record, or a redacted portion of a record, that has been omitted from an affidavit of records: Questor Technology Inc v Stagg, 2022 ABQB 578 at para 126. In the Rules, a “record” includes “the representation of or a record of any information, data or other thing that is or is capable of being represented or reproduced visually or by sound, or both” (emphasis added). Records are often thousands of pages. Further, records will often contain both relevant and material, and irrelevant, information. [42] Further, the parties must ensure that the removal of irrelevant information does not render records misleading or incomprehensible or creates unfairness.
